observations: Process lifecycle: created (forked, not yet scheduled) → running → sleeping (interruptible/uninterruptible) → stopped (SIGSTOP/SIGTSTP) → zombie (exited, parent hasn't wait()ed) → reaped. /proc/<pid>/status State field reports the kernel's view ('R', 'S', 'D', 'T', 'Z'). 'D' (uninterruptible) typically means a syscall is blocked in IO and cannot be killed even by SIGKILL — most common cause of unkillable processes.

name: linux.primitives.zombie-reaping
observations: Zombie reaping: Process that exited but whose exit-status hasn't been collected by its parent via wait(2)/waitpid/waitid stays as a zombie (/proc entry with State=Z, no other resources). PID-1 of a namespace is responsible for reaping orphans (children whose original parent exited and were reparented). Without a reaper, zombies accumulate until pid-max — the 'docker zombie problem' tini/dumb-init solves.

name: linux.primitives.subreaper
observations: Subreaper (PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER): Per-process attribute: when set, orphaned descendants reparent to this process instead of pid 1. Lets a service supervisor catch its own grandchildren without needing to actually be pid 1. systemd uses this for user@.service scope.

name: linux.primitives.wait-syscalls
observations: wait/waitpid/waitid family: Syscalls that retrieve a child's exit status: wait(2) — any child; waitpid(2) — specific PID or process group; waitid(2) — full siginfo + flexible WNOHANG/WNOWAIT options. Required to reap zombies. SIGCHLD is delivered to the parent on child exit/stop/continue (configurable via sigaction's SA_NOCLDSTOP / SA_NOCLDWAIT).

name: linux.primitives.signal-delivery-actions
observations: Signal default actions: Per-signal default behavior when no handler installed: Term (terminate), Core (terminate + dump core), Ign (ignore), Stop (suspend), Cont (resume). E.g. SIGTERM=Term, SIGKILL=Term (uncatchable), SIGSEGV=Core, SIGCHLD=Ign, SIGSTOP=Stop, SIGCONT=Cont. signal(7) tabulates all 64.

name: linux.primitives.signal-realtime
observations: Realtime signals: SIGRTMIN..SIGRTMAX (typically 32 signals). UNLIKE standard signals, RT signals queue (multiple deliveries don't merge), are delivered in priority order (lowest number first), and carry a sigval payload via sigqueue(3). RLIMIT_SIGPENDING caps the per-user queue depth. Used by glibc internally (NPTL thread cancellation, timers); rarely by app code.

name: linux.primitives.cgroup-procs-vs-threads
observations: cgroup.procs vs cgroup.threads: cgroup.procs adds a process (and all its threads) to the cgroup. cgroup.threads adds a single thread (requires the cgroup's type to be 'threaded'). 'threaded' cgroups can only contain threads of a single process and only thread-aware controllers (cpu, perf_event, pids) work. The default 'domain' type is what containers use.

name: linux.primitives.cgroup-events
observations: cgroup.events file: Per-cgroup file exposing 'populated' (any descendant has processes) and 'frozen' (cgroup.freeze=1 took effect) flags. Watchable via inotify or the file's poll interface — the canonical way to wait for 'cgroup is empty' (e.g., systemd's main-PID death detection).

name: linux.primitives.cgroup-freeze
observations: cgroup freeze: Atomically suspends every process in a cgroup (and descendants). Write 1 to cgroup.freeze. Useful for snapshot consistency, debugging, CRIU-style checkpoint. Replaces the v1 freezer controller; works on every v2 cgroup without requiring a special controller.

name: linux.primitives.memory-overcommit
observations: Memory overcommit: vm.overcommit_memory sysctl: 0 (heuristic: refuse obviously-too-large allocs), 1 (always allow — never NULL from malloc), 2 (strict: total commit ≤ vm.overcommit_ratio% of RAM + swap). Heuristic mode (default) is why Java often gets MAP_FAILED only when actually touching pages; strict mode is recommended for memory-sensitive servers. malloc()=NULL ↔ touched-page=OOM-kill is the consequence chain.

name: linux.primitives.virtual-memory-areas
observations: Virtual memory areas (VMAs): Per-process list of mapped regions: text, data, heap, stack, mmap'd files, shared libraries, anonymous mmaps. Visible in /proc/<pid>/maps (path + start-end + perms + offset + dev:inode). RLIMIT_AS caps total VMA size; vm.max_map_count limits the count (some apps need it raised — Elasticsearch is the famous case).

name: linux.primitives.thread-group-id
observations: Thread group ID (TGID): The PID of the first thread in a process; same value returned by getpid() in every thread of that process. The kernel's per-thread ID is what /proc/<pid>/task/<tid> uses; TGID = the user-visible 'process' identifier. This is why 'ps -L' shows multiple lines per process and 'top -H' splits threads.

name: linux.primitives.process-state-running
observations: Process state R (running): On CPU or runnable on the run queue. /proc/<pid>/status State='R (running)'. Doesn't necessarily mean currently executing — could be waiting for a CPU.

name: linux.primitives.process-state-sleeping
observations: Process state S (interruptible sleep): Blocked in a syscall waiting for an event, but signal-deliverable. /proc/<pid>/status State='S (sleeping)'. Most idle daemons (sshd, init) live here.

name: linux.primitives.process-state-disk-sleep
observations: Process state D (uninterruptible sleep): Blocked in kernel, signals deferred. Cannot be killed (even SIGKILL doesn't interrupt). Usually a syscall stuck in IO (NFS hang, slow disk, broken USB). /proc/<pid>/status State='D (disk sleep)'. The 'reboot to recover' state.

name: linux.primitives.process-state-stopped
observations: Process state T (stopped): Suspended via SIGSTOP/SIGTSTP/SIGTTIN/SIGTTOU or by ptrace tracer. Resumed by SIGCONT. /proc/<pid>/status State='T (stopped)' or 't (tracing stop)'.

name: linux.primitives.process-state-zombie
observations: Process state Z (zombie): Exited; awaiting wait() by parent. Holds only the /proc/<pid>/ entry — no memory, no FDs. /proc/<pid>/status State='Z (zombie)'. Accumulates if pid-1 doesn't reap (the docker zombie problem).

name: linux.primitives.process-state-dead
observations: Process state X (dead): Process is being torn down by the kernel — transient state never visible to ps/top under normal conditions.

name: linux.primitives.process-state-traced
observations: Process state t (tracing stop): Stopped by ptrace tracer (e.g. strace, gdb attached). Distinct from 'T' (signal-induced stop) in /proc/<pid>/status.

name: linux.primitives.signal-state-pending
observations: Signal state: pending: Signal delivered but not yet handled because mask blocks it. SigPnd and ShdPnd lines in /proc/<pid>/status. Standard signals collapse multiple pending into one; RT signals queue.

name: linux.primitives.signal-state-blocked
observations: Signal state: blocked: In the per-thread signal mask — pending instead of delivered. SigBlk in /proc/<pid>/status.

name: linux.primitives.signal-state-ignored
observations: Signal state: ignored: Disposition is SIG_IGN — kernel discards on delivery. SigIgn in /proc/<pid>/status. Note: PID 1 ignores ALL signals it has no handler for, even if disposition is SIG_DFL — see pid-1-init-semantics.

name: linux.primitives.signal-state-caught
observations: Signal state: caught: User-installed handler will run on delivery. SigCgt in /proc/<pid>/status.

name: linux.primitives.cgroup-state-populated
observations: cgroup state: populated: At least one descendant cgroup contains a process. Visible as `populated 1` in cgroup.events. Useful signal for service supervisors to detect that all child processes have exited.

name: linux.primitives.cgroup-state-frozen
observations: cgroup state: frozen: cgroup.freeze=1 has fully taken effect — every process in subtree is suspended. Visible as `frozen 1` in cgroup.events. Atomic relative to syscall entry (in-progress syscalls complete; new ones block until thaw).

name: linux.primitives.cgroup-subsystem
observations: cgroup subsystem: The kernel's process grouping + resource control framework. Code under kernel/cgroup/. Provides the cgroupfs interface mounted at /sys/fs/cgroup. Per-controller subsystems (memory, cpu, io, pids, hugetlb, rdma, misc, cpuset, cgroup-bpf) plug in via the cgroup_subsys interface.

name: linux.primitives.namespace-subsystem
observations: namespace subsystem: Kernel infrastructure providing the 8 namespace types. Per-namespace data structures hang off task_struct->nsproxy. Lifetime is reference-counted; namespace dies when last process referencing it (including via /proc/<pid>/ns/* open FDs and bind-mounts) exits.

name: linux.primitives.lsm-subsystem
observations: LSM subsystem: Kernel framework for stackable mandatory access control. Modules register hook implementations called at security-relevant points (file open, exec, mmap, capability check, etc.). Order in which LSMs run is configurable via lsm= boot parameter. Active LSMs visible in /sys/kernel/security/lsm.

name: linux.primitives.keyrings-subsystem
observations: keyrings subsystem: In-kernel key storage and management. Code under security/keys/. Used by dm-crypt (LUKS key passing), NFSv4 idmap, ecryptfs, fscrypt, and any service needing secrets the kernel itself uses without exposing them to userspace.

name: linux.primitives.signals-subsystem
observations: signals subsystem: Kernel infrastructure for asynchronous notification of processes. Per-thread sigqueue + per-process shared queue. Signal delivery happens at syscall return / interrupt return / scheduler entry. Code in kernel/signal.c.

name: linux.primitives.pthreads-subsystem
observations: NPTL pthreads implementation: glibc's POSIX threads layer (Native POSIX Thread Library). Maps each pthread to a kernel task (1:1 model, replacing the older M:N LinuxThreads). Uses futexes for fast user-space synchronization (mutex, cond, rwlock, barrier).

name: linux.primitives.oom-killer-subsystem
observations: OOM killer subsystem: Kernel code (mm/oom_kill.c) that selects victims when memory is exhausted. Per-cgroup OOM killer in cgroup v2 + memory.max constraints; global OOM kicks in when entire host hits a wall. Score function blends RSS, oom_score_adj, and other factors; recursion through ancestor cgroups when MemoryHigh/Max are set.

name: linux.primitives.seccomp-subsystem
observations: seccomp subsystem: The secure-computing (syscall filtering) facility. Code in kernel/seccomp.c. Plugs into syscall entry to evaluate the filter chain before syscall execution. Audit integration logs SECCOMP_RET_LOG actions to auditd.

name: linux.primitives.proc-sys-tree
observations: /proc/sys (sysctl tree): Procfs subtree exposing kernel tunables — vm.*, kernel.*, fs.*, net.* (ownership of net.* belongs in linux/networking). Read/write via /proc/sys/<path> or via sysctl(8). Persistent settings in /etc/sysctl.conf or /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf.

name: linux.primitives.proc-pid-ns
observations: /proc/<pid>/ns/* namespace links: Magic symlinks identifying each namespace the process belongs to. setns(2) takes an open FD on these. Bind-mountable to keep a namespace alive after its last process exits.

name: linux.primitives.proc-pid-uid-map
observations: /proc/<pid>/uid_map: User namespace UID translation table. Format: 'inside-uid host-uid count' lines. Write-once after process is in a userns. Companion: /proc/<pid>/gid_map (with /proc/<pid>/setgroups gating).

name: linux.primitives.proc-pid-cgroup
observations: /proc/<pid>/cgroup: Per-process cgroup membership. Format: 'hierarchy-id:controller-list:cgroup-path'. v2 entries have hierarchy-id 0 and empty controller-list. Quick way to see which cgroup (and thus which container) a PID belongs to.

name: linux.primitives.proc-pid-status
observations: /proc/<pid>/status: Human-readable per-process state. Lines: Name, State, Tgid, Pid, PPid, Uid (real/eff/saved/fs), Gid, FDSize, VmPeak/VmSize/VmRSS/VmData/VmStk, Threads, NSpid (PIDs in each namespace), CapInh/CapPrm/CapEff/CapBnd/CapAmb (capability sets as hex), Seccomp (0/1/2), SigQ/SigPnd/ShdPnd/SigBlk/SigIgn/SigCgt (signal masks).

name: linux.primitives.sysfs-cgroup
observations: /sys/fs/cgroup (cgroupfs mount point): Standard mount point for the cgroup pseudo-filesystem. v2: a single tree. v1: per-controller subdirs (cpu/, memory/, blkio/, …). systemd manages the layout: /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/<unit>/, user.slice/user-<uid>.slice/, …

name: linux.primitives.etc-security-limits
observations: /etc/security/limits.conf: PAM-honored ulimit defaults set at login. Per-user/group soft and hard limits for nofile, nproc, fsize, memlock, stack, etc. Effective only for sessions opened via PAM (login, sshd, su); systemd-managed services use the unit's LimitX= directives instead.

name: linux.primitives.proc-cmdline
observations: /proc/cmdline: Read-only view of the kernel command line booted with. Source for diagnosing 'is X enabled?' (e.g. cgroup_no_v1=, systemd.unified_cgroup_hierarchy=, mitigations=, root=).

name: linux.primitives.oom-killer-driver
observations: OOM killer policy: The kernel selects an OOM victim by scoring every task: oom_score = scaled RSS + oom_score_adj * (totalpages / 1000). Highest non-immune (oom_score_adj != -1000) wins. Per-cgroup OOM (memory.oom.group=1) kills every process in the cgroup atomically. Global OOM picks across the whole system.

name: linux.primitives.keyring-default-driver
observations: Default keyring lookup order: When a key is requested without an explicit keyring: thread-keyring → process-keyring → session-keyring → user-session-keyring → user-keyring → user-default-session-keyring → group-keyring (if any). request_key(2) follows this chain and may invoke /sbin/request-key to instantiate a missing key from userspace.

name: linux.primitives.cgroup-v2-memory-events
observations: memory.events file: Per-cgroup memory pressure event counters. Lines: low (memory.low breached), high (memory.high triggered throttling), max (memory.max hit, leading to OOM if reclaim fails), oom (cgroup OOM occurred), oom_kill (count of processes killed by cgroup OOM). Watching memory.events with inotify is how systemd-oomd / oomd act before global OOM kicks in.

name: linux.primitives.cgroup-v2-cpu-stat
observations: cpu.stat file: Per-cgroup CPU accounting. Fields: usage_usec (total CPU time), user_usec, system_usec, nr_periods (CFS periods elapsed), nr_throttled (periods throttled), throttled_usec (time spent throttled). When user reports 'CPU is throttled even though usage is low', this is where the truth is.

name: linux.primitives.cgroup-v2-io-stat
observations: io.stat file: Per-cgroup per-device IO accounting. Lines: '<major>:<minor> rbytes=N wbytes=N rios=N wios=N dbytes=N dios=N'. Doesn't include filesystem-cache hits — only IO that hit the block layer.

name: linux.primitives.mount-propagation-shared
observations: MS_SHARED mount propagation: Default for systemd-managed roots. New mounts propagate bidirectionally between peer mounts. Containers that bind-mount /var/lib/docker would see (and be seen by) the host's view if propagation isn't reset.

name: linux.primitives.mount-propagation-private
observations: MS_PRIVATE mount propagation: No mount events propagate. The runc default for the container's root after pivot_root — container mounts are isolated from host.

name: linux.primitives.mount-propagation-slave
observations: MS_SLAVE mount propagation: Receives propagation from master peer group, doesn't propagate back. Useful for /sys/fs/cgroup inside containers — host cgroup remounts visible inside, container mounts stay inside.

name: linux.primitives.mount-propagation-unbindable
observations: MS_UNBINDABLE mount propagation: Cannot be the source of a bind-mount. Niche — used to prevent escape via mount manipulation in unusual setups.

name: linux.primitives.prctl-no-new-privs
observations: PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS feature: The prctl operation that sets the no_new_privs bit. Permanent (cannot be cleared). Inherited across fork/exec. Required for unprivileged seccomp filter installation. Foundation of confined process startup.

name: linux.primitives.prctl-child-subreaper
observations: PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER feature: prctl operation marking a process as the reaper for orphaned descendants. Lets a service manager catch SIGCHLD for grandchildren without becoming pid 1.

name: linux.primitives.prctl-securebits
observations: PR_SET_SECUREBITS feature: Capability-system tweaks: SECBIT_NOROOT (UID 0 doesn't get root caps), SECBIT_NO_SETUID_FIXUP (no cap manipulation on UID change), SECBIT_KEEP_CAPS (preserve P set across UID change to non-zero), and locked variants. Each has a *_LOCKED counterpart that prevents future changes.

name: linux.primitives.setpriority-nice
observations: setpriority(2)/nice(2): Adjust per-process scheduling 'nice' value (-20 to +19; lower = higher priority). Non-CAP_SYS_NICE callers can only raise nice (lower priority). Affects CFS share allocation. systemd's `Nice=` directive.

name: linux.primitives.ionice-prio
observations: ionice / IO scheduling priority: Per-process IO scheduling class: real-time (0), best-effort (1, default), idle (3). Tunable via ioprio_set(2) syscall or ionice(1). Applies under CFQ/BFQ schedulers; less impact under mq-deadline/none.

name: linux.primitives.sched-setaffinity
observations: sched_setaffinity(2): Pin a process/thread to a subset of CPUs. Inherited across fork. Container runtimes use this for `--cpuset-cpus`. Inverse: sched_getaffinity gets the current mask.

name: linux.primitives.setsid-setpgrp
observations: setsid(2)/setpgid(2): Process group / session manipulation. setsid creates a new session (process becomes session leader, no controlling terminal). setpgid moves a process between groups for job control. Used by daemons to detach from terminal at startup.

name: linux.networking.tcp-protocol
observations: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol): Reliable, ordered, byte-stream transport over IP. RFC 793. Connection-oriented (3-way handshake SYN/SYN-ACK/ACK; 4-way close FIN/ACK/FIN/ACK). Flow control via receive window; congestion control via cwnd (Reno/Cubic/BBR). The default for HTTP, SSH, most application protocols. Linux implementation surfaces in tcp(7) man page; tunable via setsockopt with SOL_TCP / TCP_* options and sysctls under net.ipv4.tcp_*.

name: linux.networking.udp-protocol
observations: UDP (User Datagram Protocol): Connectionless message-oriented transport. RFC 768. No reliability, ordering, or congestion control — sender writes a datagram, kernel sends one packet. DNS queries, NTP, QUIC's underlying transport, RTP, syslog over UDP. Per-message-boundary semantics; recvfrom returns one datagram. Linux: udp(7) man page; SO_RCVBUF/SO_SNDBUF still apply.

name: linux.networking.ipv4-protocol
observations: IPv4: Version 4 Internet Protocol. 32-bit addresses (4.3 billion). Header includes TTL, fragmentation, ToS, source/dest. Linux IPv4 stack in net/ipv4/. ip(7) covers BSD-socket interface; sysctls under net.ipv4.* tune behavior.

name: linux.networking.ipv6-protocol
observations: IPv6: Version 6 Internet Protocol. 128-bit addresses, simplified header, no fragmentation by routers (path MTU discovery), built-in IPsec support. Linux IPv6 stack in net/ipv6/. ipv6(7) man page; net.ipv6.* sysctls.

name: linux.networking.unix-domain-protocol
observations: Unix domain sockets: Local IPC over the filesystem. Stream (SOCK_STREAM), datagram (SOCK_DGRAM), or seqpacket (SOCK_SEQPACKET) semantics. Identified by a filesystem path (or abstract namespace prefixed with \0). Faster than TCP loopback (no IP/transport-layer overhead). Used by Docker socket /var/run/docker.sock, DBus, systemd, X11.

name: linux.networking.netlink-protocol
observations: Netlink: Bidirectional kernel↔userspace message channel. Family AF_NETLINK. Subprotocols include NETLINK_ROUTE (interface/route mgmt — what `ip` uses), NETLINK_NETFILTER (nftables, conntrack), NETLINK_AUDIT, NETLINK_GENERIC. Replaces ioctl as the modern way to manage kernel networking subsystems.

name: linux.networking.packet-protocol
observations: Packet (raw layer-2) sockets: Family AF_PACKET. Direct access to layer-2 frames, bypassing the IP stack. Used by tcpdump (libpcap), wireshark, DHCP clients (need to send before having IP), and anything implementing its own L2 protocol. PF_PACKET socket types: SOCK_RAW (full ethernet), SOCK_DGRAM (cooked, no eth header).

name: linux.networking.arp-protocol
observations: ARP (Address Resolution Protocol): Maps IPv4 addresses to MAC (Ethernet) addresses on a local link. RFC 826. Request: 'who has 10.0.0.5?' broadcast; reply: 'I do, MAC=...'. ARP cache (`ip neigh show`) per-netns. Stale or poisoned entries break L3 connectivity even when L1/L2 are fine.

name: linux.networking.ndp-protocol
observations: NDP (Neighbor Discovery Protocol, IPv6): IPv6 equivalent of ARP. Uses ICMPv6 messages (Neighbor Solicitation, Neighbor Advertisement, Router Solicitation, Router Advertisement). Also handles router discovery and SLAAC.

name: linux.networking.dns-protocol
observations: DNS: Domain Name System. Hierarchical name → record (A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, NS, SOA, PTR, SRV) lookup. Default UDP/53 (TCP/53 for AXFR/large responses), DoT TCP/853, DoH HTTPS/443. Linux client-side: glibc's resolver (configured via /etc/resolv.conf), nsswitch (which DBs to consult), or systemd-resolved.

name: linux.networking.ethernet-protocol
observations: Ethernet (L2): Layer-2 frame format. 6-byte src+dst MAC, optional 802.1Q VLAN tag, EtherType (0x0800 IPv4, 0x86dd IPv6, 0x0806 ARP, 0x88cc LLDP), payload, FCS. The default L2 on every Linux interface; bridges connect ethernet segments at L2.

name: linux.networking.vlan-protocol
observations: VLAN (802.1Q): Layer-2 segmentation via 4-byte tag inserted between MAC and EtherType. 12-bit VID (0-4095). Linux: `ip link add link eth0 name eth0.10 type vlan id 10`. Each VLAN gets its own subinterface; bridges can forward by VID.

name: linux.networking.vxlan-protocol
observations: VXLAN: Virtual eXtensible LAN. L2-over-UDP overlay (default UDP/4789). 24-bit VNI (16M virtual networks). Used by Docker overlay driver, Kubernetes Calico/Flannel for pod networking across nodes.

name: linux.networking.gre-protocol
observations: GRE (Generic Routing Encapsulation): L3 tunneling protocol (IP protocol 47). Encapsulates arbitrary L3 in IP. Linux: `ip tunnel add gre0 mode gre remote ... local ...`. Used in some VPN setups and SDN underlays.

name: linux.networking.ipsec-protocol
observations: IPsec: IP security suite (AH for authentication, ESP for encryption+auth). Tunnel or transport mode. Linux: XFRM framework configured via `ip xfrm`. Strongswan/wireguard-go alternatives common.

name: linux.networking.tls-protocol
observations: TLS: Transport Layer Security. RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3). On TCP. Provides encryption + authentication + integrity. Linux's KTLS offload (CONFIG_TLS) does symmetric crypto in-kernel for sendfile() throughput. Most application TLS is in userspace via OpenSSL/GnuTLS.

name: linux.networking.dhcp-protocol
observations: DHCP: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol. UDP/67-68. Client broadcasts DISCOVER → server OFFER → client REQUEST → server ACK. Linux clients: dhclient, dhcpcd, systemd-networkd's built-in DHCP. Container-runtime IP allocation usually IPAM (Docker/CNI), not DHCP.

name: linux.networking.tcp-state-listen
observations: TCP state: LISTEN: Server socket waiting for incoming SYN. Created by listen(2). `ss -tln` shows; `ss -tlpn` adds owning PID. Backlog queue depth from listen()'s 2nd arg, capped by net.core.somaxconn.

name: linux.networking.tcp-state-syn-sent
observations: TCP state: SYN_SENT: Client has sent SYN, awaiting SYN-ACK. If kernel retries (net.ipv4.tcp_syn_retries) elapse without response, connect() returns ETIMEDOUT.

name: linux.networking.tcp-state-syn-recv
observations: TCP state: SYN_RECV: Server received SYN, sent SYN-ACK, awaiting client ACK. SYN-cookie protection avoids per-half-open-conn allocation under SYN flood (net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies).

name: linux.networking.tcp-state-established
observations: TCP state: ESTABLISHED: Bidirectional data flow possible. Where the bulk of socket lifetime is. `ss -t` shows.

name: linux.networking.tcp-state-fin-wait1
observations: TCP state: FIN_WAIT_1: Local side sent FIN; awaiting remote's ACK or remote's FIN. After local close().

name: linux.networking.tcp-state-fin-wait2
observations: TCP state: FIN_WAIT_2: Local FIN ACKed; awaiting remote's FIN. Stuck connections here usually mean remote app hasn't closed.

name: linux.networking.tcp-state-time-wait
observations: TCP state: TIME_WAIT: Active closer waits 2*MSL (~60-120s on Linux) before fully releasing the 4-tuple. Prevents delayed segments from a previous incarnation polluting a new connection. High TIME_WAIT count = client-side process making many short connections; tune via tcp_tw_reuse, ephemeral port range, or app-level connection pooling.

name: linux.networking.tcp-state-close-wait
observations: TCP state: CLOSE_WAIT: Remote sent FIN; local has ACKed but local app hasn't called close(2). Stuck in CLOSE_WAIT = file-descriptor leak in local app.

name: linux.networking.tcp-state-closed
observations: TCP state: CLOSED: Connection fully torn down. The kernel removes the socket entry. Briefly visible in /proc/net/tcp before cleanup.

name: linux.networking.socket-type-stream
observations: Socket type SOCK_STREAM: Reliable byte-stream socket. Implies TCP for AF_INET/AF_INET6, stream-style for AF_UNIX. read()/write() may return short — caller must loop.

name: linux.networking.socket-type-dgram
observations: Socket type SOCK_DGRAM: Message-boundary preserving socket. Implies UDP for AF_INET; datagram unix-socket for AF_UNIX. Each recv() returns at most one datagram (truncates if buffer too small).

name: linux.networking.socket-type-seqpacket
observations: Socket type SOCK_SEQPACKET: Sequenced, reliable, message-boundary preserving (best of stream + datagram). Used by AF_UNIX SOCK_SEQPACKET.

name: linux.networking.address-family
observations: Address family / protocol family: socket(2)'s first arg. AF_INET (IPv4), AF_INET6 (IPv6), AF_UNIX/AF_LOCAL (unix domain), AF_NETLINK (kernel ↔ user), AF_PACKET (raw L2), AF_BLUETOOTH, AF_CAN (CAN bus). Determines address layout and protocol choice constraints.

name: linux.networking.port-binding
observations: Port binding: bind(2) attaches a socket to a local address+port. Without explicit bind, kernel picks an ephemeral (net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range). Privileged ports (<1024) require CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE. EADDRINUSE if already bound; EADDRNOTAVAIL if address not on a local interface.

name: linux.networking.connection-establishment
observations: Connection establishment (3-way handshake): client SYN → server SYN-ACK → client ACK. Then both sides ESTABLISHED. connect(2) on the client returns when ACK arrives (or timeout). accept(2) on the server returns the new socket once the third ACK arrives.

name: linux.networking.connection-teardown
observations: Connection teardown (4-way handshake): close(2) → FIN → ACK from peer → peer's close → FIN → ACK. Both sides traverse FIN_WAIT_1/FIN_WAIT_2/CLOSE_WAIT/LAST_ACK/TIME_WAIT depending on who closed first. Half-closed state via shutdown(2) SHUT_WR.

name: linux.networking.ephemeral-port-range
observations: Ephemeral port range: net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range — port range kernel picks for outbound connections that didn't explicitly bind. Default ~32768-60999. Exhaustion → connect() returns EADDRNOTAVAIL.

name: linux.networking.path-mtu-discovery
observations: Path MTU Discovery: Sender starts with interface MTU; routers may reply ICMP 'fragmentation needed' with the next hop's MTU. Linux records discovered MTU per route. Broken if intermediate firewalls drop ICMP — black-hole problem manifests as 'small packets work, large hang'. tcp_mtu_probing sysctl enables a fallback probing mechanism.

name: linux.networking.tcp-window-scaling
observations: TCP window scaling: RFC 1323 option allowing the 16-bit receive-window field to be scaled by a factor (up to 14). Required for high-bandwidth-delay-product links. net.ipv4.tcp_window_scaling=1 default. NAT or middlebox stripping the option breaks throughput on long-RTT links.

name: linux.networking.tcp-congestion-control
observations: TCP congestion control: Algorithm choosing send rate to avoid network collapse. Linux ships reno, cubic (default since 2.6.19), bbr, dctcp, vegas, illinois. Per-socket override via TCP_CONGESTION sockopt; default via net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control. Default 'cubic' is good general-purpose; 'bbr' wins on bufferbloat-prone paths.

name: linux.networking.tcp-keepalive
observations: TCP keepalive: After tcp_keepalive_time idle (default 7200s), kernel sends probes every tcp_keepalive_intvl (default 75s). After tcp_keepalive_probes failures (default 9), connection is reset. Per-socket override via SO_KEEPALIVE + TCP_KEEPIDLE/TCP_KEEPINTVL/TCP_KEEPCNT.

name: linux.networking.tcp-fastopen
observations: TCP Fast Open: RFC 7413. Carries application data in the SYN packet, eliminating one RTT for repeat connections. Server replies with a TFO cookie in SYN-ACK; subsequent connections from same client present the cookie to authenticate early-data. net.ipv4.tcp_fastopen sysctl (1=client, 2=server, 3=both).

name: linux.networking.tcp-syn-cookies
observations: TCP SYN cookies: net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies. When the SYN queue overflows (under SYN flood), encode connection state into the SYN-ACK ISN — no per-half-open allocation. Slight performance penalty, immune to half-open SYN floods. Default 1 since Linux 2.4.

name: linux.networking.so-reuseaddr-vs-reuseport
observations: SO_REUSEADDR vs SO_REUSEPORT: REUSEADDR: bind() doesn't error if same address is in TIME_WAIT or different-but-overlapping (wildcard vs specific). REUSEPORT (Linux 3.9+): MULTIPLE listening sockets can bind the SAME port — kernel load-balances incoming connections across them via 4-tuple hash. The high-throughput accept() pattern.

name: linux.networking.tcp-nodelay-nagle
observations: Nagle's algorithm vs TCP_NODELAY: Nagle (default ON) buffers small writes until previous data is ACKed, reducing tinygram overhead. Hurts latency-sensitive small-write workloads. TCP_NODELAY=1 disables Nagle. TCP_CORK is opposite — actively coalesce until uncorked. SSH, interactive protocols set NODELAY; bulk transfer benefits from default.

name: linux.networking.tcp-cork
observations: TCP_CORK: Linux-specific. While set, kernel buffers writes (up to ~200ms) before sending. Useful when you'll write multiple small chunks and want them coalesced into one segment. Common pattern: SET_CORK → sendfile + write_header → CLEAR_CORK.

name: linux.networking.netfilter-hook-chain
observations: Netfilter hook chain: Per-protocol-family chain of hook points: PREROUTING, INPUT, FORWARD, OUTPUT, POSTROUTING. Packets traverse hooks in fixed order; iptables/nftables register rules at hook points. Knowing the chain order is essential for understanding why a rule didn't match.

name: linux.networking.iptables-table
observations: iptables table: Tables group rules by purpose: filter (default — ACCEPT/DROP/REJECT), nat (DNAT/SNAT/MASQUERADE), mangle (TOS/TTL/marks), raw (NOTRACK before conntrack), security (SELinux integration). Each table has its own copy of relevant chains.

name: linux.networking.iptables-chain
observations: iptables chain: Per-table linear list of rules. Built-in chains: INPUT (to local), OUTPUT (from local), FORWARD (transit), PREROUTING (before routing), POSTROUTING (after routing). User-defined chains for grouping. Default policy applies if no rule matches.

name: linux.networking.iptables-rule-match-target
observations: iptables match-and-target: Rule = match criteria (-p, -s, -d, --sport, --dport, -i, -o, --state, --syn, etc.) + jump target (-j ACCEPT/DROP/REJECT/LOG/MASQUERADE/...). First matching rule's target executes (unless target returns).

name: linux.networking.nat-snat
observations: SNAT (Source NAT): Rewrites the source IP/port of outbound packets at POSTROUTING. e.g. private 10.0.0.0/8 → public IP. MASQUERADE is the auto-pick-source variant (for dynamic IPs like DSL/cable).

name: linux.networking.nat-dnat
observations: DNAT (Destination NAT): Rewrites the destination IP/port at PREROUTING. The mechanism behind 'docker -p 8080:80' (incoming :8080 → container :80). Conntrack remembers the original tuple so reply packets get rewritten back.

name: linux.networking.conntrack-table
observations: Conntrack (connection tracking) table: Per-namespace table of all flows kernel is tracking. Required for stateful filtering (`-m state ESTABLISHED,RELATED`) and NAT (so reply packets get reverse-translated). nf_conntrack_max bounds size; full table = new connections drop. `conntrack -L` lists; `cat /proc/net/nf_conntrack` raw.

name: linux.networking.conntrack-timeouts
observations: Conntrack timeouts: Per-protocol per-state timeouts. nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_established = 5 days default — too short for keepalive-less long-lived TCP connections through firewalls. ESTABLISHED expiring kills the conn for the firewall but not for endpoints (resulting in RST when traffic resumes).

name: linux.networking.nft-family
observations: nftables family: Top-level grouping. inet (IPv4+IPv6 unified), ip (IPv4 only), ip6 (IPv6 only), arp, bridge, netdev (per-interface ingress/egress at lowest level). 'inet' is the modern default for dual-stack rules.

name: linux.networking.nft-table-chain-rule
observations: nftables table → chain → rule hierarchy: nft rule lives in a chain, which lives in a table (in a family). Chains hook into netfilter (type filter/nat/route, hook input/output/forward/prerouting/postrouting, priority N). Rules within evaluated top-down. More flexible than iptables fixed schema.

name: linux.networking.nft-set-map
observations: nftables sets and maps: Named sets store discrete values (IPs, ports, MACs); maps store key→value. Lookup is O(log n) (red-black tree backend). Replaces the iptables ipset hack. Allows e.g. `ip saddr @blocklist drop` against a dynamic set updated from userspace.

name: linux.networking.routing-table
observations: Routing table: Per-netns set of routes. Linux supports multiple tables (named in /etc/iproute2/rt_tables, indexed 0-255). Default 'main' (254) holds normal routes; 'local' (255) holds local interface addresses; rules in `ip rule` decide which table to consult per packet. `ip route` shows; `ip route get <dst>` evaluates.

name: linux.networking.policy-routing
observations: Policy routing (ip rule): Per-packet route-table selection by source/destination/fwmark/iif/oif. `ip rule add from 10.0.0.0/8 lookup 100`. Enables multi-homing with per-source default routes.

name: linux.networking.veth-pair
observations: veth pair: Virtual ethernet — pair of back-to-back interfaces. Packet in one comes out the other. The standard mechanism for connecting a network namespace to the host (one end stays in host bridge, other end goes into the netns). Created via `ip link add type veth peer name ...`.

name: linux.networking.bridge-device
observations: Bridge (Linux bridge): In-kernel L2 switch. Multiple interfaces attached as ports; bridge learns MACs and forwards frames. STP optional (off by default). docker0, virbr0 are bridges. bridge(8) configures STP/VLAN-filtering/per-port settings beyond what `ip link` exposes.

name: linux.networking.tap-tun-device
observations: TAP / TUN devices: Userspace ↔ kernel virtual interfaces. TUN: L3 (IP packets); TAP: L2 (Ethernet frames). OpenVPN/WireGuard use TUN (route packets to userspace VPN process); QEMU uses TAP (give VM an L2 interface).

name: linux.networking.bonding-aggregation
observations: Bonding (link aggregation): Combine multiple NICs into one logical interface for HA or throughput. Modes: active-backup, balance-rr, balance-xor, 802.3ad (LACP), broadcast, balance-tlb, balance-alb. Configured via `ip link add bond0 type bond` + per-slave attach.

name: linux.networking.tc-qdisc
observations: tc qdisc: Queueing discipline — algorithm controlling order/timing of packet transmission on an interface. pfifo_fast (default for older kernels), fq_codel (modern default — fairness + bufferbloat reduction), htb (hierarchical token bucket — for rate limits), cake (modern fq+aqm). Configured via tc qdisc add. (Detail in linux/networking-advanced; tc(8) man page is bulky enough that we don't ingest it in this leaf — see Phase 1.5).

name: linux.networking.epoll-edge-vs-level
observations: epoll edge-triggered vs level-triggered: EPOLLET = edge-triggered: events fire ONCE on state change; you must drain the socket fully (until EAGAIN) before re-entering epoll_wait. Level-triggered (default) keeps firing while data is pending. ET is more efficient at scale but trickier — most application-server bugs in this area are ET-related.

name: linux.networking.epoll-vs-select-poll
observations: epoll vs select/poll: select/poll have O(N-monitored-FDs) per call. epoll registers FDs once (epoll_ctl) and returns only those with events (epoll_wait). For thousands of long-lived connections, epoll is dramatically faster.

name: linux.networking.somaxconn
observations: net.core.somaxconn (listen-queue ceiling): Hard ceiling on the SOMAXCONN argument to listen(2)'s backlog. App passes a value; kernel min(app-value, somaxconn). If somaxconn is too low, accept queue overflows during connection bursts → connections dropped (visible as ListenOverflows in /proc/net/netstat).

name: linux.networking.so-rcvbuf-sndbuf
observations: SO_RCVBUF / SO_SNDBUF: Per-socket receive/send buffer size in bytes. Auto-tuning in modern kernels (tcp_rmem/tcp_wmem range). Setting to small value can cap throughput on long-RTT links (BDP > buffer = stall).

name: linux.networking.dns-resolver-glibc
observations: glibc resolver: libresolv: reads /etc/resolv.conf at first lookup, caches. Honors search domains, options (timeout, attempts, single-request, ndots, edns0, rotate). nsswitch.conf decides which databases (files, dns, mdns) and order. Most processes use it transparently via getaddrinfo(3).

name: linux.networking.dns-systemd-resolved
observations: systemd-resolved: Local DNS stub on 127.0.0.53. Caching, DNSSEC, DoT support, multi-NIC awareness (per-link DNS). nsswitch entry 'resolve' or symlink /etc/resolv.conf → /run/systemd/resolve/stub-resolv.conf. resolvectl(1) inspects.

name: linux.networking.ndots
observations: resolv.conf 'ndots' option: Threshold for relative-vs-absolute name lookups. ndots=N: if a query has fewer than N dots, try search-list suffixes first. Default 1. Kubernetes' default ndots=5 explodes lookup count for FQDN-like internal names — common source of surprise DNS latency.

name: linux.networking.netfilter-subsystem
observations: netfilter subsystem: Kernel framework for packet filtering, NAT, mangling. Provides the hook points; iptables and nftables are userspace tools that program rules at those hooks. Per-netns rule tables (so each container has its own iptables view).

name: linux.networking.iptables-subsystem
observations: iptables subsystem: Legacy userspace tool + kernel modules (xt_*, ipt_*) for netfilter rule programming. Mature, ubiquitous, but linear-scan rule lookup. Being replaced by nftables but still ships everywhere.

name: linux.networking.nftables-subsystem
observations: nftables subsystem: Modern netfilter front-end. Single CLI (nft), unified inet family for v4+v6, sets/maps with O(log n) lookup, atomic ruleset replace. Default on RHEL 8+, Debian 11+. iptables-nft compat layer exists.

name: linux.networking.conntrack-subsystem
observations: conntrack subsystem: nf_conntrack module. Tracks every flow's state for stateful filtering and NAT. Per-netns table. Tunable via sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_*.

name: linux.networking.socket-api-subsystem
observations: BSD socket API subsystem: socket(2)/bind(2)/listen(2)/accept(2)/connect(2)/send(2)/recv(2)/close(2)/setsockopt(2)/getsockopt(2)/shutdown(2). The interface every networking application uses. Implementations per address family.

name: linux.networking.iproute2-subsystem
observations: iproute2 (ip command suite): User-space tool suite (`ip`, `ss`, `tc`, `bridge`, `nstat`) replacing the older net-tools (ifconfig, route, netstat, arp). Talks to kernel via NETLINK_ROUTE. Only sane interface for IPv6, multiple routing tables, policy routing.

name: linux.networking.dns-resolver-subsystem
observations: DNS resolver subsystem (NSS+resolv): Userspace stack: glibc's nsswitch dispatcher → per-DB modules (files, dns via libresolv, resolve via systemd-resolved). Determines name → address resolution for getaddrinfo(3).

name: linux.networking.epoll-subsystem
observations: epoll subsystem: Scalable I/O readiness notification. epoll_create1(2), epoll_ctl(2), epoll_wait(2). Per-CPU red-black trees of monitored FDs. The basis of every modern Linux event loop (libuv, libev, tokio).

name: linux.networking.firewall-subsystem
observations: firewalld / ufw / shorewall: Higher-level firewall managers built on iptables/nftables. firewalld (zone-based, RHEL/Fedora default). ufw (uncomplicated, Ubuntu default). shorewall (declarative). Each generates lower-level rules; mixing with raw iptables can fight.

name: linux.networking.socket-syscall
observations: socket(2) syscall: Create an endpoint for communication. Returns a FD. Args: domain (AF_*), type (SOCK_*), protocol (usually 0 = default for type).

name: linux.networking.bind-syscall
observations: bind(2) syscall: Assign a local address+port to a socket. Required before listen() (server) or for clients wanting a specific source.

name: linux.networking.listen-syscall
observations: listen(2) syscall: Mark a stream socket as passive (server). Backlog arg sets the SYN+accept queue depths (kernel uses min(backlog, somaxconn)).

name: linux.networking.accept-syscall
observations: accept(2) / accept4(2) syscall: Dequeue a completed connection from the listen-socket's accept queue, returning a new connected socket. Blocks if queue empty (unless O_NONBLOCK). accept4 adds flag arg (SOCK_NONBLOCK, SOCK_CLOEXEC) — race-free atomic alternative to accept+fcntl.

name: linux.networking.connect-syscall
observations: connect(2) syscall: Initiate a connection. For TCP, sends SYN, blocks for handshake (or returns EINPROGRESS if O_NONBLOCK). For UDP, sets default destination so subsequent send() works.

name: linux.networking.send-recv-syscalls
observations: send(2)/recv(2)/sendto/recvfrom/sendmsg/recvmsg: Data transfer. send/recv on connected sockets; sendto/recvfrom carry per-call destination/source; sendmsg/recvmsg pass scatter-gather + ancillary data (SCM_RIGHTS for FD passing over AF_UNIX, IP_PKTINFO for source-address selection).

name: linux.networking.setsockopt-getsockopt-syscalls
observations: setsockopt(2)/getsockopt(2) syscalls: Per-socket option get/set. Args: socket FD, level (SOL_SOCKET, IPPROTO_TCP, IPPROTO_IP, IPPROTO_IPV6), option name, value buffer. Where SO_REUSEADDR / TCP_NODELAY / IP_BIND_ADDRESS_NO_PORT etc. are set.

name: linux.networking.shutdown-syscall
observations: shutdown(2) syscall: Half-close a socket. SHUT_RD (no more reads), SHUT_WR (no more writes — sends FIN), SHUT_RDWR (both). Distinct from close() which releases the FD entirely.

name: linux.networking.epoll-syscalls
observations: epoll_create1/epoll_ctl/epoll_wait syscalls: epoll_create1 makes an epoll instance (FD); epoll_ctl adds/modifies/deletes monitored FDs; epoll_wait blocks until events or timeout. The Linux high-performance event loop primitive.

name: linux.networking.poll-select-syscalls
observations: poll(2)/select(2)/pselect: Older readiness-multiplexing syscalls. Pass a list of FDs each call (vs epoll's persistent registration). poll() uses pollfd struct (no FD_SETSIZE limit); select() is bit-mask based and limited to FD_SETSIZE (1024). pselect adds atomic sigmask swap.

name: linux.networking.netlink-route-driver
observations: NETLINK_ROUTE driver: netlink subprotocol for interface/route/neighbor/qdisc/filter management. The thing `ip` and `tc` talk to. Notifications also flow back (interface up/down, address add/remove, route change).

name: linux.networking.netlink-netfilter-driver
observations: NETLINK_NETFILTER driver: netlink subprotocol for nftables, conntrack, ulogd. nft uses it to install rulesets; conntrack(8) uses it to query/modify the conntrack table.

name: linux.networking.bridge-driver
observations: Linux bridge driver: In-kernel L2 switch implementation. Forwards frames between attached interfaces. MAC learning, STP, VLAN-filtering modes. Heart of docker0 and most VM networking.

name: linux.networking.bonding-driver
observations: bonding driver: Link aggregation. Loaded as bonding module. Mode + per-mode params via /sys/class/net/bondN/bonding/* or systemd-networkd's [Bond] section.

name: linux.networking.tun-tap-driver
observations: TUN/TAP driver: Universal virtual interface. Userspace process opens /dev/net/tun, configures via TUNSETIFF ioctl, then read/write packets. Used by VPNs, VMs, container userspace networking (slirp4netns).

name: linux.networking.proc-net-tcp
observations: /proc/net/tcp{,6}: All IPv4 (and v6) TCP sockets, with state, local/remote addr, queue depths, owning UID, inode. Read by ss(8) and netstat. Hex-encoded; ss does the decoding for you.

name: linux.networking.proc-net-udp
observations: /proc/net/udp{,6}: UDP sockets enumeration. Same shape as /proc/net/tcp.

name: linux.networking.proc-net-unix
observations: /proc/net/unix: Unix-domain sockets. Lists Inode + RefCount + Protocol + Flags + Type + State + Path. ss -x parses.

name: linux.networking.proc-net-dev
observations: /proc/net/dev: Per-interface byte/packet counters (rx/tx, errors, drops, fifo, frame). What ifconfig and `ip -s link` parse. drops > 0 = receive ring overflow, often hint that net.core.rmem_max needs raising or NIC driver tuning.

name: linux.networking.proc-net-route
observations: /proc/net/route: Hex-encoded IPv4 routing table. `route` parses (deprecated); `ip route` uses NETLINK_ROUTE instead.

name: linux.networking.proc-net-arp
observations: /proc/net/arp: IPv4 ARP cache. `arp -a` parses. Modern equivalent: `ip neigh show`.

name: linux.networking.proc-net-snmp
observations: /proc/net/snmp: Per-protocol counters in SNMP-MIB names: TcpExt (tcp extended stats), TcpInSegs, TcpRetransSegs, IpInDelivers, etc. nstat(8) parses to a friendly form. Source of TCP retransmit %, listen-queue-overflow counters.

name: linux.networking.proc-net-netstat
observations: /proc/net/netstat: Extended counters not in /proc/net/snmp. ListenOverflows (full accept queue), ListenDrops, TCPSynRetrans, TCPLossUndoUuse, etc. Read by `nstat -as`.

name: linux.networking.iptables-feature-state-match
observations: iptables -m state / -m conntrack: Stateful filtering. -m state --state ESTABLISHED,RELATED accepts return traffic and conntrack-related packets (FTP data conn, ICMP errors). The cornerstone of 'allow established' firewall rules.

name: linux.networking.iptables-feature-recent
observations: iptables -m recent: Per-IP rate-limit / temporary blocklist within iptables. e.g. SSH brute-force protection: count attempts per IP, drop when threshold exceeded for a window.

name: linux.networking.iptables-feature-limit
observations: iptables -m limit: Token-bucket rate limit on rule match. e.g. log only 5 packets/sec to avoid log flooding.

name: linux.networking.nft-feature-meta
observations: nftables 'meta' selector: Match on packet metadata: meta iif/oif (interface), meta mark (fwmark), meta priority (skb priority), meta length, meta nftrace, meta cgroup (cgroup ID).

name: linux.networking.nft-feature-ct
observations: nftables 'ct' (conntrack) selector: Match on conntrack state: ct state established/related/new/invalid; ct status; ct mark.

name: linux.networking.tcpdump-feature-bpf-filter
observations: tcpdump BPF filter expression: libpcap filter language compiled to cBPF for in-kernel packet matching. Syntax: `host`, `port`, `src`, `dst`, `tcp`, `udp`, `icmp`, `ip`, `ip6`, boolean operators. Used by tcpdump, wireshark, raw libpcap apps.

name: linux.networking.tcpdump-feature-write-pcap
observations: tcpdump -w to pcap file: Capture to a .pcap file for offline analysis (wireshark, tshark, tcpdump -r). Combined with -C (size rotate) and -W (file count) for ring-buffer captures.

name: linux.networking.so-bindtodevice
observations: SO_BINDTODEVICE: Bind a socket to a specific interface name (e.g. 'eth0'). Bypasses normal routing — packets only on that interface. Requires CAP_NET_RAW. Used by VPN clients to send packets out a specific tunnel.

name: linux.networking.ip-bind-address-no-port
observations: IP_BIND_ADDRESS_NO_PORT: Defer port assignment from bind() to connect(). Lets bind() reserve a source IP without consuming an ephemeral port — the kernel picks per-destination at connect() time, allowing far more concurrent outbound connections to a single dest:port. Critical for high-fanout proxies.

name: linux.networking.so-mark-fwmark
observations: SO_MARK / fwmark: Per-packet 32-bit mark stored in skb->mark. Set per-socket via SO_MARK (requires CAP_NET_ADMIN), or via iptables/nft 'meta mark set'. Used by policy routing (`ip rule add fwmark X lookup Y`).

name: linux.networking.cgroup-net-cls
observations: net_cls cgroup (v1): Per-cgroup network class id, written to skb->priority for tc filters. v1 only — v2 uses BPF cgroup hooks instead. Largely obsolete in modern container setups.

name: linux.networking.icmp-protocol
observations: ICMP / ICMPv6: Internet Control Message Protocol. RFC 792 (v4) / RFC 4443 (v6). Carries diagnostic and error messages: echo request/reply (ping), destination unreachable, time exceeded (TTL=0, used by traceroute), redirect, fragmentation needed. Not a transport in the BSD-sockets sense — opened via raw sockets.

name: linux.networking.raw-socket-protocol
observations: Raw IP sockets: Family AF_INET/AF_INET6 with type SOCK_RAW. Lets userspace assemble and send IP packets with custom headers. Requires CAP_NET_RAW. Used by ping, traceroute (when implemented as raw rather than ICMP), nmap.

name: linux.networking.socket-type-raw
observations: Socket type SOCK_RAW: Raw socket — packet-level access. Requires CAP_NET_RAW. AF_INET SOCK_RAW = raw IP; AF_PACKET SOCK_RAW = raw L2.

name: linux.debugging.ebpf
observations: eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter): In-kernel virtual machine running verified, JIT-compiled programs at hook points: kprobes, uprobes, tracepoints, perf events, syscall entry/exit, network XDP/tc, cgroup ingress/egress, LSM hooks, sockets. Replaces classic BPF (cBPF) for nearly everything except seccomp filters. The instrumentation primitive behind bpftrace, BCC, Cilium, Falco, Pixie, Hubble. CAP_BPF (5.8+) needed to load programs; CAP_PERFMON for tracing-class.

name: linux.debugging.kprobes
observations: kprobes: Dynamic instrumentation that attaches a handler at any kernel instruction address (with a few denylisted instructions). Pre-handler runs before the instruction, post-handler after. Programmable via kernel module, perf-probe(1), or eBPF. The kernel-side hook every dynamic-tracing tool builds on.

name: linux.debugging.uprobes
observations: uprobes: Userspace dynamic instrumentation. Attaches at a virtual address inside a binary's text; on hit, kernel notifies the tracer (perf, eBPF). The mechanism behind tracing arbitrary userspace functions without modifying the binary. Used by USDT (User Statically Defined Tracing) probes too.

name: linux.debugging.ftrace
observations: ftrace: Built-in kernel function tracer. Plug-in tracers: function (call graph at function entry), function_graph (entry+exit with timing), nop, sched_switch, irqsoff, preemptoff, wakeup. Controlled via /sys/kernel/debug/tracing/ files. trace-cmd(1) is the user-friendly front-end. Used for kernel function-call latency analysis.

name: linux.debugging.tracepoint
observations: Tracepoint (static): Compile-time instrumentation point in the kernel — predefined named events (sched_switch, sched_wakeup, irq_handler_entry, syscalls/sys_enter_*, mm/page_alloc, etc.). Stable kernel ABI (unlike kprobes which depend on internal symbols). Subscribed via perf, ftrace, eBPF.

name: linux.debugging.perf-event-counter
observations: perf event counter: Hardware (PMU) and software counters tracked per-process or per-CPU. perf_event_open(2) syscall opens an FD; perf(1) wraps. Common: cycles, instructions, cache-references, cache-misses, branch-instructions, branch-misses, page-faults, context-switches, cpu-migrations.

name: linux.debugging.flame-graph
observations: Flame graph: Brendan Gregg-popularized stack-trace visualization: x-axis = aggregated samples, y-axis = stack depth, width = relative cost. Generated from `perf record -g` → `perf script` → flamegraph.pl. The standard CPU-profile rendering.

name: linux.debugging.kdump
observations: kdump: Kernel-crash dump mechanism. At boot, reserve memory via crashkernel= cmdline; on panic, kexec into a separate 'capture' kernel which writes /proc/vmcore (the panicked kernel's memory) to disk. Typical handler: makedumpfile(8) compresses, then crash(8) analyzes.

name: linux.debugging.kexec
observations: kexec (fast kernel switch): Switch to a different kernel without firmware reboot. Used by kdump (crashkernel boots the capture kernel via kexec from a panic context) and live kernel updates.

name: linux.debugging.audit-framework
observations: Linux audit framework: Kernel audit subsystem + auditd userspace daemon. Records syscall / file-watch / privilege events to /var/log/audit/audit.log. Rules via auditctl. Queries via ausearch/aureport. SELinux/AppArmor denials surface here as AVC records.

name: linux.debugging.dynamic-debug
observations: Dynamic debug (dyndbg): Runtime control of pr_debug() statements in kernel. Enable per-file/function/line via /sys/kernel/debug/dynamic_debug/control. Useful for activating verbose driver logging without rebuilding kernel.

name: linux.debugging.bpf-program-types
observations: BPF program types: Each program type defines what context (hook) it runs in: BPF_PROG_TYPE_KPROBE, _UPROBE, _TRACEPOINT, _PERF_EVENT, _XDP, _SCHED_CLS (tc), _CGROUP_SOCK, _LSM, _SOCK_FILTER (cBPF). Determines available helpers + verifier rules.

name: linux.debugging.bpf-maps
observations: BPF maps: Key-value stores accessible from BPF programs and userspace. Types: HASH, ARRAY, PERCPU_HASH/ARRAY, LRU_HASH, RINGBUF, PERF_EVENT_ARRAY, STACK_TRACE, CGROUP_ARRAY. The mechanism for BPF programs to keep state and ship results to userspace.

name: linux.debugging.bpf-verifier
observations: BPF verifier: Static analyzer the kernel runs on every loaded BPF program. Verifies all branches halt, no out-of-bounds memory access, no unbounded loops, kernel pointer dereferences are safe. Verifier failures are notoriously hard-to-debug ('R1 invalid mem access', 'value pointer arithmetic prohibited').

name: linux.debugging.usdt-probe
observations: USDT (User Statically Defined Tracing): DTrace-style static probes embedded in user binaries. PostgreSQL, MySQL, OpenJDK, Node, Python, Ruby ship with USDT probes. Hooked via uprobes; bpftrace 'usdt:<binary>:<probe>' syntax.

name: linux.debugging.lttng-tracer
observations: LTTng (Linux Trace Toolkit Next Generation): Production-grade tracer (kernel + userspace). Lower overhead than ftrace under heavy event volume; per-CPU lockless ring buffers. Used in telecom/embedded for always-on production tracing. Out of scope for this leaf (sparse coverage in our corpus).

name: linux.debugging.gdb-debugger
observations: GDB (GNU debugger): Source-level debugger for C/C++/Rust/Go (and many others via runtime support). Breakpoints (`break`), watchpoints (`watch`), single-step, backtrace, register/memory inspection, multi-thread, multi-process, remote-debug via gdbserver, core-dump postmortem. Works with -g compiled binaries.

name: linux.debugging.crash-utility
observations: crash (vmcore analyzer): Postmortem kernel debugger. Reads vmcore (kdump output) + System.map + vmlinux. Commands: bt (backtrace), kmem (kernel memory), files, mount, log, irq, runq, rd (read raw memory), sym, dis (disassemble). The standard tool for analyzing kernel panics from production hosts.

name: linux.debugging.strace-tool
observations: strace (syscall tracer): Trace syscalls via ptrace(2). Output: syscall name + arg decoding + return value/errno. Powerful for 'why is this program failing': open() returning ENOENT (file missing), connect() returning ECONNREFUSED, etc. -c summarizes; -e to filter; -f to follow forks.

name: linux.debugging.ltrace-tool
observations: ltrace (library call tracer): Like strace but for shared-library function calls. Useful when bug is in libfoo's API rather than the syscall layer. Lower volume than strace usually.

name: linux.debugging.lsof-tool
observations: lsof (list open files): Lists every open FD in the system: regular files, dirs, sockets, pipes, devices, deleted-but-still-open files. The 'who has /var/log/foo.log open?' tool. -p PID, -c COMMAND, -i :PORT, -u USER.

name: linux.debugging.htop-tool
observations: htop (interactive process viewer): Curses-based real-time process monitor. Color-coded CPU/mem bars, tree view, filter (F4), sort (F6), kill (F9), nice/renice. Configurable column set. Replaces top for interactive use.

name: linux.debugging.dmesg-ringbuffer
observations: Kernel ring buffer (dmesg): Circular buffer of kernel printk messages — boot logs, OOM killer, segfaults, hardware errors, driver messages. dmesg(1) reads /dev/kmsg. journald also captures and rotates. The first place to look on weird kernel-related symptoms.

name: linux.debugging.iostat-tool
observations: iostat: Per-device disk I/O statistics from /proc/diskstats. Columns: tps (transactions/s), kB_read/s, kB_wrtn/s, %util (saturation). -x adds extended (await, svctm, %iowait). sysstat package; pairs with sar for historical.

name: linux.debugging.iotop-tool
observations: iotop: Per-process I/O usage (like top, but for disk I/O). Reads /proc/<pid>/io. Requires CAP_NET_ADMIN (for taskstats netlink) — typically run as root. Diagnoses 'which process is hammering the disk?'

name: linux.debugging.vmstat-tool
observations: vmstat: System-wide virtual memory + processes + IO + CPU stats sampled at interval. Procs (r/b), Memory (swpd/free/buff/cache), Swap (si/so), IO (bi/bo), System (in/cs), CPU (us/sy/id/wa/st). Quick triage tool: high si/so = swapping; high wa = IO bound.

name: linux.debugging.pidstat-tool
observations: pidstat: Per-process resource statistics (CPU, memory, IO, context switches, page faults). sysstat package. -d for IO, -r for memory, -w for context switches.

name: linux.debugging.blktrace-tool
observations: blktrace: Block-layer I/O tracer. Captures every IO request: queue, merge, getrq, complete, timestamps. Output → blkparse for human-readable, btt for latency analysis. Diagnoses block-layer / IO scheduler / device latency.

name: linux.debugging.bpftrace-tool
observations: bpftrace: DTrace-inspired high-level eBPF front-end. One-liner syntax: `bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_open { printf("%s\n", str(args->filename)); }'`. Compiles to BPF, attaches probes, prints aggregations (count, hist, lhist, stats). Brendan Gregg's go-to.

name: linux.debugging.numastat-tool
observations: numastat: Per-NUMA-node memory statistics. Hits, misses, foreign allocations, local allocations. Diagnoses NUMA-affinity issues on multi-socket boxes.

name: linux.debugging.makedumpfile-tool
observations: makedumpfile: Compresses raw vmcore (kdump output) by stripping zero pages, free pages, cache pages. Reduces 'memory full of zeroes' multi-GB dumps to manageable size. Companion to crash(8).

name: linux.debugging.trace-cmd-tool
observations: trace-cmd: User-friendly ftrace front-end. Commands: record, report, reset, start, stop, extract, list, snapshot. Manages /sys/kernel/debug/tracing/ for you. Output is .dat file (KernelShark can render).

name: linux.debugging.valgrind-tool
observations: Valgrind: Userspace memory error and profiling framework. Tools: memcheck (default — leak+invalid-access detection via shadow memory), helgrind/drd (race detection), cachegrind (cache modeling), callgrind (call graph), massif (heap profiling). Slows program 10-50x. Production debugging tool of choice for C/C++ memory bugs.

name: linux.debugging.ptrace-syscall
observations: ptrace(2) syscall: The kernel mechanism behind strace/gdb/ltrace. Tracer attaches to tracee; on every syscall entry/exit, signal, or memory-modifying event, tracee is suspended and tracer notified. Operations: ATTACH, DETACH, PEEKDATA, POKEDATA, GETREGS, SETREGS, CONT, SYSCALL, SINGLESTEP. Yama LSM restricts who can ptrace whom (kernel.yama.ptrace_scope).

name: linux.debugging.bpf-syscall
observations: bpf(2) syscall: Single multiplexed entry point for all BPF operations: PROG_LOAD, MAP_CREATE, MAP_LOOKUP_ELEM, MAP_UPDATE_ELEM, PROG_ATTACH, PROG_DETACH, PROG_TEST_RUN, OBJ_PIN, OBJ_GET, LINK_CREATE. CAP_BPF (5.8+) for most; CAP_PERFMON for tracing-class.

name: linux.debugging.perf-event-open
observations: perf_event_open(2) syscall: Open a counter or event source. Returns FD that can be read for counter values, mmap'd for ring buffer (sample data), or used as target for ioctl (PERF_EVENT_IOC_ENABLE/DISABLE/RESET/REFRESH/SET_FILTER/...). The syscall behind perf(1) and BCC's tracing programs.

name: linux.debugging.signal-sigsegv
observations: SIGSEGV (segmentation fault): Signal sent on invalid memory access (null deref, write to read-only, beyond mmap). Default action: dump core + terminate. siginfo.si_addr = faulting address; si_code = SEGV_MAPERR (no mapping)/SEGV_ACCERR (mapping but wrong perms)/SEGV_BNDERR (bound check)/SEGV_PKUERR (pkey).

name: linux.debugging.signal-sigabrt
observations: SIGABRT (assertion failure): Self-signal sent by abort(3) or assert(3) failure. Default: core dump + terminate. Indicates a deliberate crash from invariant violation.

name: linux.debugging.signal-sigbus
observations: SIGBUS (bus error): Memory access fault that's not a page fault — usually mmap'd file shrunk under you, or unaligned access on alignment-strict architecture, or NUMA hugepage issues.

name: linux.debugging.signal-sigfpe
observations: SIGFPE (arithmetic exception): Despite name, not just floating point — also integer divide by zero, integer overflow (when SIGFPE-on-overflow enabled), invalid float ops. siginfo.si_code distinguishes.

name: linux.debugging.core-dump
observations: Core dump: Snapshot of process memory (text, data, stack, heap, all writable mmaps) written to disk on fatal signal. Filename per /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern (or piped to systemd-coredump). RLIMIT_CORE caps size; ulimit -c 0 disables. Use gdb (or crash for kernel) to analyze.

name: linux.debugging.ringbuffer-perf
observations: perf ring buffer: mmap'd memory region holding sample records from perf events. Reader (userspace tool) consumes; producer (kernel) writes. -m/--mmap-pages controls size. Overflow drops samples (visible as PERF_RECORD_LOST).

name: linux.debugging.bpf-ringbuf
observations: BPF ring buffer (BPF_MAP_TYPE_RINGBUF): 5.8+ replacement for BPF_MAP_TYPE_PERF_EVENT_ARRAY. MPMC ring shared between BPF programs and userspace. Variable-size records, ordering preserved across CPUs. Replaces the per-CPU perf-event array for cleaner aggregation.

name: linux.debugging.proc-pid-stack
observations: /proc/<pid>/stack: Current kernel-side call stack of the process (if it's in kernel). Useful for diagnosing 'D state' (uninterruptible sleep) — see what kernel function it's stuck in.

name: linux.debugging.proc-pid-wchan
observations: /proc/<pid>/wchan: Symbolic name of kernel function the process is sleeping in. Quick read for D-state diagnosis (e.g. 'nfs_wait_on_request' = stuck waiting for NFS).

name: linux.debugging.proc-pid-syscall
observations: /proc/<pid>/syscall: Currently-executing syscall number + args. Useful for 'what's this hung process doing?' without attaching strace.

name: linux.debugging.gdb-breakpoint
observations: GDB breakpoint / watchpoint: Breakpoint: stop execution at code address. Watchpoint: stop on memory read/write/access. Hardware watchpoints use CPU debug registers (limited count, no perf cost). Software watchpoints single-step (huge perf cost). gdb auto-picks; `set can-use-hw-watchpoints 0` forces SW.

name: linux.debugging.gdb-backtrace
observations: GDB backtrace: `bt` (or `where`) prints frames from current location up the call stack. Requires DWARF debug info (-g) or at least frame pointers (-fno-omit-frame-pointer). Without either: backtrace lies (misses inlined functions, stops early).

name: linux.debugging.gdb-thread
observations: GDB threading: `info threads` lists all threads of process; `thread N` switches; `thread apply all bt` prints backtrace per thread. Combined with non-stop mode lets you debug one thread while others run.

name: linux.debugging.symbol-resolution
observations: Symbol resolution: Mapping address → function/variable name. Symbols come from ELF .symtab (full) or .dynsym (exported only). Stripping (`strip`) removes .symtab. Debug info (DWARF) lives in .debug_* sections — separable into .debuginfo files (GDB auto-loads from /usr/lib/debug/.build-id/).

name: linux.debugging.dwarf-debug-info
observations: DWARF debug info: Standard format for source-level debug info: variables, types, functions, source line numbers, frame info. Requires -g compile flag. Optional split-debug (.debug section in separate file) reduces production binary size.

name: linux.debugging.frame-pointer-vs-dwarf
observations: Frame pointer vs DWARF unwinding: Two ways to walk the stack: frame pointers (RBP/EBP register chain — small perf cost, no debug info needed) or DWARF .eh_frame info (no perf cost but requires unwinder + complete DWARF). Modern compilers default to no frame pointer for performance; `perf record -g` defaults to DWARF unwinding. -fno-omit-frame-pointer restores reliable backtraces.

name: linux.debugging.sampling-vs-tracing
observations: Sampling vs tracing: Sampling: periodically capture state (PC, stack); statistical, low overhead, may miss rare events. perf record (default) is sampling. Tracing: capture every event (every function call, every syscall); complete data, high overhead. ftrace function tracer is tracing. Different problems need different approaches.

name: linux.debugging.cpu-profile-on-cpu-vs-off-cpu
observations: On-CPU vs Off-CPU profiling: On-CPU: where time is spent computing (CPU samples while running). Off-CPU: where time is spent NOT running — blocked on IO, locks, sleep. Brendan Gregg's USE method emphasizes the off-CPU time, which classic profilers (gprof, perf record default) miss entirely.

name: linux.debugging.context-switch
observations: Context switch: CPU swap from one task to another. Voluntary: task blocked (waiting). Non-voluntary: preempted (timeslice up or higher-priority woke). High non-voluntary = CPU oversubscription. /proc/<pid>/status voluntary_ctxt_switches + nonvoluntary_ctxt_switches.

name: linux.debugging.thread-state-running
observations: Process state R (sampling): A sampler that catches a thread in state R is on-CPU. Off-CPU = anything else (S/D/T). The basis of off-CPU flame graphs: subtract on-CPU from wall time.

name: linux.debugging.audit-rule
observations: Audit rule (auditctl syntax): `-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S openat -F path=/etc/shadow -k shadow_access` = audit every openat of /etc/shadow with key 'shadow_access'. Rules persist via /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules (or audit.rules) loaded at boot.

name: linux.debugging.audit-record-types
observations: Audit record types: SYSCALL (system call), AVC (SELinux/AppArmor decision), USER_LOGIN, CRED_ACQ, ANOM_PROMISCUOUS, MAC_POLICY_LOAD, etc. Each event = group of records sharing msg-id. ausearch -m TYPE filters.

name: linux.debugging.kernel-panic
observations: Kernel panic: Unrecoverable kernel state. Kernel printk()s panic message + register dump + stack trace, then halts (or reboots if panic= sysctl set). On modern systems, kdump captures vmcore for analysis.

name: linux.debugging.kernel-oops
observations: Kernel oops: Recoverable kernel error (e.g. NULL deref in module). Kernel logs trace, taints itself, and tries to continue (often the offending task is killed). dmesg shows 'BUG:' or 'Oops:'. Tainted kernel is suspect for further bugs — bug reports require untainted kernels.

name: linux.debugging.process-d-state
observations: Process D state (uninterruptible sleep): Cannot be killed (even SIGKILL). Stuck in kernel waiting for IO completion. /proc/<pid>/stack + /proc/<pid>/wchan show what kernel function. NFS hangs, broken disks, kernel bugs land here. Often only resolution: reboot.

name: linux.debugging.process-t-state
observations: Process T state (stopped): Suspended via SIGSTOP/SIGTSTP. Resumed by SIGCONT. Sometimes seen because debugger attached (then it's 't' lowercase = traced).

name: linux.debugging.process-z-state
observations: Process Z state (zombie): Process exited; awaiting wait() by parent. Holds /proc entry only — no memory, no FDs. Common in containers when pid 1 doesn't reap (the docker init problem).

name: linux.debugging.tracer-attached-state
observations: Tracer-attached state: When ptrace() attaches, tracee state changes per signals. Visible as 't' (lowercase) in ps. Tracer must explicitly continue (PTRACE_CONT) for tracee to resume.

name: linux.debugging.bpf-program-loaded
observations: BPF program loaded state: BPF program lives in kernel after PROG_LOAD; visible via `bpftool prog show`. Detached but still loaded if no link. Pinned to bpffs to survive program exit.

name: linux.debugging.audit-enabled-state
observations: Audit enabled state: auditctl -e {0|1|2} sets audit subsystem. 0=off, 1=on, 2=on+locked (cannot disable until reboot — security mode).

name: linux.debugging.ftrace-tracer-state
observations: ftrace active tracer state: /sys/kernel/debug/tracing/current_tracer = the active plug-in tracer. Default 'nop' = disabled. Set to 'function' or 'function_graph' to capture.

name: linux.debugging.ebpf-subsystem
observations: eBPF subsystem: Kernel infrastructure: verifier, JIT compiler (per-arch), helper functions, map types, link mechanism, bpffs. Enables sandboxed in-kernel programs invoked at hook points without kernel module loading.

name: linux.debugging.perf-subsystem
observations: perf subsystem: perf_event_open(2) + per-CPU ring buffers + kernel/events/ code. Foundation of perf(1), bpf-tracing-class programs, intel-pt traces.

name: linux.debugging.ftrace-subsystem
observations: ftrace subsystem: Kernel code/trace + control files at /sys/kernel/debug/tracing/. Per-CPU ring buffers, dynamic-ftrace patches function entry to call __mcount/__fentry__ hook. Plug-in tracers (function, function_graph, irqsoff, etc.).

name: linux.debugging.kprobes-subsystem
observations: kprobes subsystem: Patches kernel instructions to call handler. Pre/post handlers, register access, kretprobes (return probes). The dynamic-trace primitive ftrace/perf/eBPF build on for non-tracepoint sites.

name: linux.debugging.uprobes-subsystem
observations: uprobes subsystem: Userspace dynamic probes. Trap inserted at virtual address; on hit, kernel notifies tracer. Usable from perf, ftrace, eBPF, USDT-aware tools.

name: linux.debugging.audit-subsystem
observations: audit subsystem: kernel/audit*.c. Ring of records sent over NETLINK_AUDIT to auditd. Rules in audit_filter_list. Per-tgid/per-syscall filtering.

name: linux.debugging.kdump-subsystem
observations: kdump subsystem: crashkernel= boot param + kexec_load(2) + crash code under arch/ for capturing memory state on panic. Capture kernel + initrd typically pre-loaded; on panic, kernel kexec()s to capture kernel which writes vmcore.

name: linux.debugging.binutils-suite
observations: binutils (objdump, nm, readelf, addr2line, strings, c++filt): GNU binary tools. objdump = disassemble + section headers; nm = list symbols; readelf = ELF structure dump; addr2line = address → file:line; strings = printable strings; c++filt = demangle C++ symbols. Indispensable for binary analysis.

name: linux.debugging.strace-subsystem
observations: strace + ptrace pipeline: strace uses ptrace(PTRACE_SYSCALL) to stop tracee at every syscall entry/exit, decode args from registers + memory, print, then resume. -k uses libunwind to capture stack at each syscall.

name: linux.debugging.gdb-subsystem
observations: GDB + gdbserver + ptrace + ELF: gdb client reads ELF + DWARF for symbol/source info; controls tracee via ptrace (or via gdbserver remote protocol). Multi-process and multi-arch.

name: linux.debugging.bcc-toolkit
observations: BCC (BPF Compiler Collection) — methodology cross-ref: Cross-reference: covered fully in `methodology` domain. iovisor/bcc — Python+Lua tracing tools (execsnoop, biolatency, opensnoop, etc.) using libbpf to compile/load BPF programs. Higher-level than bpftrace for complex programs.

name: linux.debugging.kdump-driver
observations: kdump kexec_load implementation: Per-arch kexec implementation. x86_64 reserves crashkernel= memory at boot, sets up identity-mapped page tables for the capture kernel, registers panic_notifier to invoke machine_crash_shutdown → machine_kexec.

name: linux.debugging.bpf-jit-driver
observations: BPF JIT compiler: Per-arch JIT (x86, arm64, ppc, mips, riscv) translates BPF bytecode to native machine code. Enabled by net.core.bpf_jit_enable. Hardening: net.core.bpf_jit_harden = constant blinding.

name: linux.debugging.perf-pmu-driver
observations: perf PMU driver: Per-architecture/CPU-model code that programs hardware Performance Monitoring Unit registers. Intel core PMU, AMD core PMU, ARM PMU. Limits the max simultaneous counters per CPU.

name: linux.debugging.audit-netlink-driver
observations: audit NETLINK_AUDIT driver: Bridge between kernel audit subsystem and userspace auditd. Records flow over NETLINK_AUDIT socket; auditd writes them to disk.

name: linux.debugging.coredump-driver
observations: coredump-handler driver: Kernel formats process state into ELF core file, then either writes to fs path (kernel.core_pattern starts with normal char) or pipes to userspace handler (core_pattern starts with `|`). systemd-coredump is the dominant pipe-handler.

name: linux.systemd.unit
observations: systemd unit: The fundamental managed entity. Types: service (.service), socket (.socket), target (.target), device (.device), mount (.mount), automount (.automount), swap (.swap), timer (.timer), path (.path), slice (.slice), scope (.scope). Defined by unit files at /usr/lib/systemd/system/ (vendor), /etc/systemd/system/ (admin override), /run/systemd/system/ (runtime).

name: linux.systemd.unit-file-loading-precedence
observations: Unit file loading precedence: Lookup order: /etc/systemd/system/ → /run/systemd/system/ → /usr/lib/systemd/system/. First found wins; absent earlier paths fall through. Drop-in dirs (UNIT.d/) layered on top via override.conf files. systemctl edit creates /etc/systemd/system/UNIT.d/override.conf.

name: linux.systemd.service-unit
observations: Service unit (.service): Long-running process, oneshot job, or notify-style daemon. Defined by [Service] section: ExecStart=, Type=, Restart=. Most common unit type. Lives at /etc/systemd/system/<name>.service.

name: linux.systemd.target-unit
observations: Target unit (.target): Synchronization point — a named state that other units can require/be wanted by. Replaces SysV runlevels. Examples: multi-user.target (= old runlevel 3), graphical.target (= 5), default.target (symlink to current default), basic.target (early-boot ordering anchor).

name: linux.systemd.socket-unit
observations: Socket unit (.socket): Listening socket(s) systemd opens before the associated service starts (socket activation). When a connection arrives, systemd starts the service and passes the FD. Companion .service usually has the same name. Defined by [Socket] section: ListenStream=, ListenDatagram=, Accept=.

name: linux.systemd.timer-unit
observations: Timer unit (.timer): Cron-like scheduled trigger. Activates the same-named .service (or Unit=). OnCalendar= for wall-clock; OnBootSec= / OnUnitActiveSec= for relative. systemd's replacement for cron.

name: linux.systemd.mount-unit
observations: Mount unit (.mount): Filesystem mountpoint managed by systemd. Auto-generated from /etc/fstab entries. Encoded path: e.g. /var/lib/foo → var-lib-foo.mount. Manually creatable for advanced needs (network mounts with retry).

name: linux.systemd.path-unit
observations: Path unit (.path): Activates same-named .service when a watched path changes (PathChanged=, PathExists=, PathExistsGlob=, PathModified=, DirectoryNotEmpty=). systemd's inotify-driven activation.

name: linux.systemd.slice-unit
observations: Slice unit (.slice): Cgroup container for grouping units to apply shared resource control. Hierarchy: -.slice (root) → system.slice / user.slice / machine.slice. Custom slices for resource pooling (e.g. workload.slice with MemoryMax= shared by all member services).

name: linux.systemd.scope-unit
observations: Scope unit (.scope): Like service but for processes systemd didn't fork. Used by user sessions (session-N.scope under user-UID.slice) and `systemd-run --scope`. Lifetime tracked via cgroup membership.

name: linux.systemd.unit-state-active
observations: Unit state: active: Unit running normally. Subtypes: running (process alive), exited (Type=oneshot completed RemainAfterExit=yes), waiting (Type=oneshot completed), listening (socket bound).

name: linux.systemd.unit-state-inactive
observations: Unit state: inactive: Unit stopped, dead. Default for never-started units.

name: linux.systemd.unit-state-failed
observations: Unit state: failed: Service exited non-zero, was killed by signal not in SuccessExitStatus=, hit start-limit (StartLimitBurst hit StartLimitIntervalSec), or condition check failed. systemctl reset-failed clears the latched failure.

name: linux.systemd.unit-state-activating
observations: Unit state: activating: Transitional — Type=notify waiting for sd_notify(READY=1), Type=oneshot ExecStart still running, Type=forking waiting for parent fork. Stuck here = misbehaving notify daemon or slow Exec.

name: linux.systemd.unit-state-deactivating
observations: Unit state: deactivating: Transitional — running ExecStop; if exceeds TimeoutStopSec, escalates to KillSignal then SIGKILL.

name: linux.systemd.unit-state-reloading
observations: Unit state: reloading: systemctl reload triggered ExecReload= and waiting for completion.

name: linux.systemd.unit-state-maintenance
observations: Unit state: maintenance: Older state name (rare in modern systemd) — corresponds to manual intervention required. Most failures land in 'failed' instead.

name: linux.systemd.service-type-simple
observations: Service Type=simple: Default. ExecStart= IS the main process. systemd considers unit started immediately after fork+exec. No fancy sync — just go.

name: linux.systemd.service-type-exec
observations: Service Type=exec: Like simple but waits for execve() to complete (vs just fork). Catches early exec failures. Newer (v240+) recommended default for new services.

name: linux.systemd.service-type-forking
observations: Service Type=forking: Classic Unix daemon — main process forks, parent exits, child becomes the long-running daemon. PIDFile= helps systemd track the right child. The 'old way'; prefer Type=simple/exec/notify.

name: linux.systemd.service-type-oneshot
observations: Service Type=oneshot: Runs ExecStart to completion, then unit is 'inactive (dead)' (or 'active (exited)' if RemainAfterExit=yes). Used for setup scripts, mounts, one-time migrations.

name: linux.systemd.service-type-notify
