observations: API v1 (legacy, deprecated): Legacy v1 API. Base URL `https://api.devin.ai/v1/*`. Org-scoped flat structure. Auth via `apk_user_` / `apk_` keys. No RBAC. Continues working during deprecation period; will be removed.

name: devin.api.api-version-v2
observations: API v2 (legacy enterprise, deprecated): Legacy v2 API. Base URL `https://api.devin.ai/v2/enterprise/*`. Enterprise-Admin-role only. Personal API keys only (no service keys). Continues during deprecation; lacks new features (RBAC, session attribution, cursor pagination).

name: devin.api.api-version-v3
observations: API v3 (current): Current API. Two scopes: Organization (`/v3/organizations/{org_id}/*`) and Enterprise (`/v3/enterprise/*`). Service user tokens (`cog_`). Full RBAC. Cursor-based pagination. Session attribution via `create_as_user_id`. Custom enterprise domains supported.

name: devin.api.organization-scope
observations: Organization API scope: v3 sub-API rooted at `/v3/organizations/{org_id}/*`. Manages resources within a single organization — sessions, knowledge, playbooks, secrets, schedules, service-users, audit-logs, etc. Where most integrations start.

name: devin.api.enterprise-scope
observations: Enterprise API scope: v3 sub-API rooted at `/v3/enterprise/*`. Cross-organization — analytics, audit logs, user/role/IdP-group management, billing, infrastructure (hypervisors), service-user provisioning, organization CRUD. Available to enterprise customers.

name: devin.api.create-as-user-id
observations: `create_as_user_id` (session attribution): Optional parameter on Create Session. When set, the session is attributed to the specified user — appears in their session list, counts toward their usage. Requires the `ImpersonateOrgSessions` permission on the calling service user's role.

name: devin.api.custom-enterprise-domain
observations: Custom enterprise API domain: Devin Enterprise customers with dedicated deployments replace `api.devin.ai` with their own domain (e.g., `api.your-company.devinenterprise.com`).

name: devin.api.cursor-pagination
observations: Cursor-based pagination: Pagination model used by all v3 list endpoints. Query params: `first` (page size, integer, default varies), `after` (opaque cursor; omit on first page). Response: items[], has_next_page, end_cursor, optional total. Replaces offset/limit from v1/v2.

name: devin.api.permission-rbac
observations: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC): Permission model in v3. Each endpoint is gated by a specific named permission. Service-user roles aggregate permissions. Two scopes: Enterprise permissions and Organization permissions. Enterprise service users automatically inherit corresponding org-level permissions across all orgs.

name: devin.api.permission-inheritance
observations: Enterprise→Organization permission inheritance: Enterprise service users assigned an enterprise-level role automatically get the corresponding org-level permission in every organization. Example: ViewAccountSessions grants ViewOrgSessions in all orgs.

name: devin.api.session-resource
observations: Session (API resource): The core agent-run resource. Created by POST /v3/organizations/{org_id}/sessions. Has a session_id, URL (https://app.devin.ai/sessions/<id>), status, prompt, optional title/playbook/tags/ACU-limit. Polls via Get Session; receives messages via Send Message.

name: devin.api.session-status
observations: Session status enum: Session lifecycle states. v1: running. v3 introduces more granular settled states: exit, error, suspended (and more — full schema on endpoint reference pages). Used by polling code (`while status not in {'exit','error','suspended'}: poll`).

name: devin.api.session-attachment
observations: Session attachment: File produced by a session (logs, screenshots, generated code). Listed via GET /v3/organizations/{org_id}/sessions/{session_id}/attachments — returns items[] with attachment_id, name, url. Download from `url` directly.

name: devin.api.knowledge-note-resource
observations: Knowledge note (API resource): Persistent context Devin uses across sessions. Fields: name, trigger (when this knowledge applies), body (the content). Org-level (POST /v3/organizations/{org_id}/knowledge/notes) and Enterprise-level (POST /v3/enterprise/knowledge/notes).

name: devin.api.knowledge-folder
observations: Knowledge folder (structure): Hierarchical folder structure containing knowledge notes. Counts of notes per folder retrievable via GET /v3/organizations/{org_id}/knowledge/folders.

name: devin.api.playbook-resource
observations: Playbook (API resource): Reusable instruction set Devin can be parameterized with. Fields: name, instructions, optional macro (e.g., `!plan`). Org-level + Enterprise-level. Triggers on assignment, label, comment-mention via integrations.

name: devin.api.secret-resource
observations: Secret (API resource): Stored credential referenced as `$VARIABLE_NAME` from blueprints and sessions. Org-level only (Devin's secrets dashboard). Endpoints under /v3/organizations/{org_id}/secrets.

name: devin.api.schedule-resource
observations: Schedule (API resource): Recurring or one-time auto-session trigger. Fields: prompt, cron_schedule (cron expression), timezone, is_enabled, optional notification preferences and agent selection. Org-level. Endpoint: /v3/organizations/{org_id}/schedules.

name: devin.api.idp-group-resource
observations: IdP group (API resource): Identity-provider group sync. Both enterprise and organization scope. Used for SSO-driven membership management. Endpoints CRUD groups + assign/unassign users.

name: devin.api.tag-resource
observations: Tag (session tag): User-defined string label attached to sessions. Org-allowed-tags configurable; default-tag settable. Sessions can have tags added/replaced/removed. Used for org-side categorization of agent runs.

name: devin.api.guardrail-violation-resource
observations: Guardrail violation (API resource): Tripped-policy event surfaced for compliance review. Both enterprise and org scope. Endpoint: GET /v3/organizations/{org_id}/guardrail-violations and GET /v3/enterprise/guardrail-violations.

name: devin.api.audit-log-entry
observations: Audit log entry: Tamper-evident record of an action. Both enterprise and org scope. v3: GET /v3/enterprise/audit-logs and GET /v3/organizations/{org_id}/audit-logs.

name: devin.api.consumption-cycle
observations: Consumption cycle: Billing cycle summary. Endpoint: GET /v3/enterprise/consumption/cycles. Tracks ACU usage per cycle.

name: devin.api.daily-consumption
observations: Daily consumption breakdown: Per-day ACU consumption. Multiple breakdowns: by user, by service-user, by session, by organization. Both enterprise and org scope.

name: devin.api.metric-active-users
observations: Active users metrics (DAU/WAU/MAU/custom-range): Engagement metrics. Endpoints for daily/weekly/monthly active users and a custom-date-range variant. Both enterprise and org scope.

name: devin.api.metric-pr
observations: PR metrics: Pull-request-creation analytics. Both enterprise and org scope. Endpoint: GET /v3/enterprise/metrics/prs and GET /v3/organizations/{org_id}/metrics/prs.

name: devin.api.metric-session
observations: Session metrics: Session-count/category analytics. Both enterprise and org scope. Includes sessions-by-category for richer slicing.

name: devin.api.metric-usage
observations: Usage metrics: Generic usage analytics surface. Enterprise: /v3/enterprise/metrics/usage. Organization: /v3/organizations/{org_id}/metrics/usage and ../usage-org.

name: devin.api.metric-search
observations: Search metrics: Search-related analytics. Both enterprise and org scope.

name: devin.api.queue-status
observations: Queue status: Snapshot of the session queue. Enterprise-only (GET /v3/enterprise/queue). Surfaces queueing pressure for capacity planning.

name: devin.api.role-resource
observations: Role (API resource): RBAC role aggregating permissions. Endpoint: GET /v3/enterprise/roles. Roles are assigned to users + service users.

name: devin.api.hypervisor-resource
observations: Hypervisor (API resource): Infrastructure-layer surface. Enterprise-only. GET /v3/enterprise/hypervisors. Surfaces hypervisor-level state for the customer's deployment.

name: devin.api.ip-access-list
observations: IP access list (API resource): Enterprise IP allowlist. Endpoints: GET / replace / clear. Restricts which IPs can access the customer's enterprise.

name: devin.api.session-insights
observations: Session insights: AI-generated summary/analysis of session behavior. Generated on-demand via POST endpoint; retrievable via GET. Used for after-the-fact retrospective on agent runs.

name: devin.api.repository-indexing-status
observations: Repository indexing status (API): Status of code-search index build for a repository. v2 endpoint: GET /v2/repositories/<repo>/status. Bulk index endpoint: POST /v2/repositories/bulk-index.

name: devin.api.snapshot-resource
observations: Snapshot (API resource — enterprise): Enterprise-deployment-level snapshot detail. v2 endpoint: GET /v2/snapshots/<id>. Surfaces details about a specific environment snapshot.

name: devin.api.repository-clone
observations: Repository clone (API): Programmatic clone of a repository into a Devin organization. v2 endpoint: POST /v2/organizations/<org>/clone-repository.

name: devin.api.org-group-limits
observations: Organization group limits: Per-org limits configurable by enterprise admins. Endpoints: GET / Update. Includes ACU caps and similar quotas.

name: devin.api.git-connection-resource
observations: Git connection (API resource): Per-org connection to a Git provider. Endpoint: GET /v3/organizations/{org_id}/git-providers/connections.

name: devin.api.git-permission-resource
observations: Git permission (API resource): Per-repo Git access permission. Endpoints: GET / Create / Replace / Delete / Clear under /v3/organizations/{org_id}/git-providers/permissions.

name: devin.api.error-401
observations: 401 Unauthorized: Missing/invalid Authorization header, expired/invalid API key, malformed Bearer token, or using a legacy `apk_` key with the Devin MCP server (which only accepts `cog_`). Solution: verify Authorization header.

name: devin.api.error-403
observations: 403 Forbidden: Service user lacks required permission, wrong key type for endpoint (legacy key with v3), or attempting to access resources outside scope. v2 endpoints require Enterprise Admin role.

name: devin.api.error-404
observations: 404 Not Found: Incorrect endpoint URL OR resource doesn't exist OR caller doesn't have access (returns 404 instead of 403 to prevent existence leakage).

name: devin.api.error-429
observations: 429 Too Many Requests: Rate limit exceeded. Wait + retry with backoff. Apply at the per-key or per-org level depending on endpoint.

name: devin.api.principal-types
observations: Principal types in /self response: GET /v3/self response field `principal_type` distinguishes 'service_user' from 'user'. For service users, populates service_user_id, service_user_name, org_id (or null for enterprise-scoped service users that span orgs).

name: devin.enterprise.deployment-cloud
observations: Enterprise Cloud deployment: Default enterprise deployment model. Brain + DevBox both run in Cognition Cloud. Public network or IP-allowlist for customer resource access. Fastest setup (minutes). Works when SCM (GitHub.com / GitLab.com / Azure DevOps Cloud) and artifact stores are public or IP-whitelistable. Does NOT support MFA VPN access to customer resources.

name: devin.enterprise.deployment-dedicated
observations: Customer Dedicated Deployment: Single-tenant Cognition-managed VPC for customers with private networks that cannot support IP allowlisting. Brain stays in Cognition Cloud; DevBox runs in customer-isolated VPC. Connects via AWS PrivateLink (preferred) or IPSec tunnel. Supports MFA VPN access to internal resources and OpenVPN.

name: devin.enterprise.brain
observations: Devin Brain (Cognition Cloud): Stateless cloud-based service powering Devin's intelligence. ALWAYS resides in Cognition Cloud (similar to GitHub Copilot's architecture). Pairs with the DevBox (which can be in customer-dedicated VPC under that deployment model).

name: devin.enterprise.aws-privatelink
observations: AWS PrivateLink (Customer Dedicated networking): Preferred secure-tunnel option between customer VPC and Cognition's single-tenant VPC for Customer Dedicated deployments. Alternative: IPSec tunnel.

name: devin.enterprise.devinapps-domain
observations: *.devinapps.com end-user domain: Domain serving Devin's interactive session tools (IDE / VSCode frontend, Desktop / browser viewer) loaded via iframes in the user's browser. End-user workstations must be able to reach `*.devinapps.com` over HTTPS/443 — corporate proxies/firewalls must allowlist it.

name: devin.enterprise.cross-tenant-websocket
observations: Cross-tenant WebSocket startup: On startup, Devin establishes a secure WebSocket connection from the customer DevBox to an isolated container in Cognition's tenant. All subsequent operations occur over this secure channel. Backend session isolation enforced.

name: devin.enterprise.compound-ai-system
observations: Compound AI system (no third-party LLM keys): Devin is described in the FAQ as a compound AI system. Does NOT currently support customer-supplied third-party LLM API keys. The Brain owns model selection.

name: devin.enterprise.rollout-mode-not-enabled
observations: Rollout mode — Not enabled: Initial state for declarative environment configuration before enterprise activation. No orgs see environment pages; all use classic setup. Activation requires Cognition admin contact.

name: devin.enterprise.rollout-mode-testing
observations: Rollout mode — Testing: Baseline rollout state after activation. Only manually opted-in orgs use blueprints. All other orgs remain on classic setup with no UI changes. Enterprise admin opts orgs in from the Rollout page. Used for piloting blueprint configuration in isolation.

name: devin.enterprise.rollout-mode-available
observations: Rollout mode — Available: Self-service rollout state. Org admins on classic setup see a migration callout on their Machine Configuration page and can self-service migrate. No automatic switch — opt-in only. Useful for awareness + paced migration.

name: devin.enterprise.rollout-mode-enabled-by-default
observations: Rollout mode — Enabled by default: Final rollout state. New orgs default to declarative blueprints. Existing orgs that were on classic with repos receive automatic classic overrides as a safety mechanism. PERMANENT action — cannot be undone without a Cognition administrator.

name: devin.enterprise.per-org-override
observations: Per-org rollout override: Enterprise admin can opt individual orgs in (Testing/Available mode) or out (Enabled by default mode) from the Rollout page's per-org table. Switches an org between blueprints and classic setup. Both blueprint and classic configs are preserved during switches.

name: devin.enterprise.automatic-classic-override
observations: Automatic classic override: Safety mechanism activated when switching to Enabled-by-default mode. Any org currently on classic setup AND with repositories configured automatically receives an explicit classic override — nothing changes for them. Orgs without repos (or already on blueprints) are unaffected.

name: devin.enterprise.migration-assistant
observations: Migration assistant (classic → declarative): Devin-driven assistant that inspects an org's existing snapshot and generates equivalent blueprint configuration. Lowers the per-org migration burden. Documented at /onboard-devin/environment/migration.

name: devin.enterprise.rollout-kpi-dashboard
observations: Rollout KPI dashboard: Top-of-Rollout-page summary metrics: Blueprint orgs (count), Rollout percentage (% on blueprints), Build health (aggregate status across blueprint orgs).

name: devin.enterprise.per-org-rollout-table
observations: Per-org rollout table: Detailed table on the Rollout page showing every org with: Organization, State (Blueprints|Classic), Override (yes/no), Classic repos (count), Blueprint repos (count), Latest build status. Filterable by All / Blueprints / Classic / Overrides.

name: devin.enterprise.three-tier-blueprint-hierarchy
observations: Three-tier blueprint hierarchy (additive): Enterprise → Organization → Repository. Additive (lower tiers don't replace upper). Enterprise blueprint runs first (baseline), then org, then repo. Knowledge items from all tiers are collected; multiple tiers can define same-named knowledge item without overwriting.

name: devin.enterprise.enterprise-blueprint
observations: Enterprise blueprint: Enterprise-tier blueprint at Settings > Devin's base environment. Default home for: standard language runtimes, security tools, corporate certificates, internal CLIs, proxy settings, registry auth. Recommended pattern: put it here unless a specific reason to scope narrower.

name: devin.enterprise.enterprise-secret
observations: Enterprise secret: Secret defined at the enterprise tier. Available in EVERY build and EVERY session across ALL organizations, in enterprise/org/repo blueprint steps alike. Managed in Settings > Devin's base environment > Secrets. Requires ManageAccountResources permission.

name: devin.enterprise.enterprise-wide-rebuild
observations: Enterprise-wide rebuild: Cascading rebuild from the enterprise tier across ALL organizations. Triggered by enterprise-blueprint update, secret rotation, or post-security-patch refresh. Each org's build runs with updated enterprise blueprint + own org/repo blueprints. Respects per-org build queue (queues behind in-progress; cancels-and-replaces queued).

name: devin.enterprise.cascading-secret-precedence
observations: Cascading secret precedence: Secrets cascade through enterprise → org → repo with more specific tiers winning on name collision. Use to override enterprise-wide credentials with team-specific tokens that have different permissions.

name: devin.enterprise.role-organization-level
observations: Organization-level role (RBAC): Org-by-org assigned RBAC role. Built-in roles: Admin (full org access), Member (standard), DeepWiki Only (DeepWiki + AskDevin + index repos only). Assignment via Org Settings > Organization Members. Custom org roles created from Enterprise Settings > Roles by users with Manage Account Membership permission.

name: devin.enterprise.role-account-level
observations: Account-level (enterprise) role (RBAC): Enterprise-wide role applying across all organizations. Users with account-level roles automatically inherit corresponding org-level permissions in every org they belong to. Built-in: Admin, Member.

name: devin.enterprise.idp-group-auto-assign
observations: IdP group → role auto-assignment: Enterprise feature mapping IdP groups to Devin roles. When users authenticate via SSO, they automatically receive the role assigned to their IdP group. Configured in Enterprise Settings > Members. Requires SSO provider to send the `groups` array in the SSO assertion.

name: devin.enterprise.sso-okta
observations: SSO via Okta (OpenID Connect): Enterprise SSO option configured against an Okta tenant via OIDC.

name: devin.enterprise.sso-azure-ad
observations: SSO via Azure AD: Enterprise SSO option for Azure AD / Entra ID.

name: devin.enterprise.sso-saml
observations: SSO via generic SAML 2.0: Enterprise SSO option for any generic SAML 2.0 identity provider.

name: devin.enterprise.sso-oidc-generic
observations: SSO via generic OIDC: Enterprise SSO option for any generic OpenID Connect provider.

name: devin.enterprise.trust-center
observations: Trust Center (trust.cognition.ai): Public security-posture surface at https://trust.cognition.ai. Documents SOC 2 Type II findings, security policies, and certifications.

name: devin.enterprise.soc2-type-ii-sept-2024
observations: SOC 2 Type II (September 2024): Cognition's SOC 2 Type II certification obtained in September 2024 (the enterprise-overview cites this date; the admin-security page cites March 2024 — likely Type I → Type II progression). Covers data security, privacy, processing integrity, confidentiality, availability.

name: devin.enterprise.dedicated-deployment-data-residency
observations: Dedicated/on-prem data residency: For Enterprise customers using dedicated or on-prem deployments, ALL customer data is stored within the customer's own tenant. Cognition does not train on this data regardless of opt-in.

name: devin.enterprise.build-health-review-cadence
observations: Weekly build-health review cadence: Recommended best-practice cadence: check build health weekly across all orgs. Look for: Failed builds (critical, blocks all repos), Partial builds (some repos failing — usually dependency/blueprint drift), Stale builds (unusually old latest-build — possibly stuck queue).

name: devin.enterprise.template-library
observations: Blueprint template library: Curated copy-paste blueprint templates for Python, Node.js, Go, Java, Ruby, Rust, advanced patterns. Located at /onboard-devin/environment/templates. Used internally by enterprise admins to share standard configs across teams.

name: devin.enterprise.audit-log-rollout
observations: Audit-logged rollout transitions: All rollout state transitions are recorded in audit logs. Captures: enterprise mode changes (Testing → Available, Enabled-by-default activation), per-org override changes (opt-in / opt-out / removal), the admin who made each change, and timestamp.

name: devin.enterprise.concurrency-conflict-rejection
observations: Concurrency-protected state transitions: If another admin changes enterprise rollout state between page-load and submit, the request is rejected with a conflict error. Prevents accidental overwrites in multi-admin environments.

name: devin.product.swe-check
observations: SWE-Check (10x faster bug detection): Cognition-built specialized model for fast bug detection in PRs. 10x faster than the prior approach. Powers the Devin Review bug-catcher with confidence-level labeling. Latency-optimized vs full agent runs.

name: devin.product.swe-1-6-model
observations: SWE-1.6 (Cognition's coding model): Cognition's specialized coding model. Improvements over predecessors: parallel tool calls, better UX, RL-scaled training. Available in Devin for Terminal alongside Opus 4.7 and GPT-5.5.

name: devin.product.single-threaded-write
observations: Single-threaded write: Coordination pattern where multiple agents may read/explore in parallel but only one agent writes at a time. Cognition's documented multi-agent learning: parallel writes don't work; serial writes with parallel review do.

name: devin.product.multi-agent-fleet
observations: Multi-agent fleet (managed Devins): Pattern of running multiple coordinated Devin sessions. Devin can now Manage Devins — coordinator-style spawning of subordinate agents. Includes scheduling Devins via cron (`Devin can now Schedule Devins`).

name: devin.product.computer-use
observations: Computer Use: Screen + keyboard/mouse automation surface for Devin. Lets the agent interact with arbitrary GUI applications inside DevBox. Recent surface — failure modes still being characterized.

name: devin.product.skills
observations: Skills (product feature): Reusable agent capabilities surfaced through the Skills product guide. Used to encapsulate complex multi-step procedures as named, reusable units.

name: devin.product.session-insights
observations: Session Insights: Per-session analysis surface. Shows ACU usage, timeline, agent decisions. Generated on-demand via API; surfaced in the Devin webapp post-session.

name: devin.product.scheduled-sessions
observations: Scheduled Sessions: Cron-driven recurring or one-time agent sessions. Configured per org via the Schedules API (or UI). Triggered by cron expression + timezone.

name: devin.product.session-tools
observations: Devin Session Tools: Debugging primitives + command palette available within an active session. Used for low-level inspection of session state.

name: devin.product.slash-commands
observations: Slash commands (in session): Primary user lever inside a session. Slash-prefixed commands invoke specific behaviors / modes. Documented at /work-with-devin/slash-commands.

name: devin.product.ask-devin-feature
observations: Ask Devin: Quick-question codebase Q&A surface. Answers via indexed-repo context. Org-level permission `Use Ask Devin`. Lower-cost alternative to a full session.

name: devin.product.knowledge-feature
observations: Knowledge (product feature, distinct from blueprint knowledge): Persistent context Devin uses across sessions — architecture docs, conventions, team workflows. Distinct from blueprint `knowledge` section (short command refs). Per-repo: Devin only sees knowledge for the repo it's working on. Configurable in Settings > Devin's Settings > Knowledge.

name: devin.product.bot-comment-settings
observations: Bot comment settings: Configurable PR comment rendering — controls how Devin's PR comments appear (verbosity, formatting, attribution).

name: devin.product.testing-and-recordings
observations: Testing and Recordings: Replay/repro feature. Records session interactions for later replay or debugging.

name: devin.product.sdlc-integration
observations: SDLC integration patterns: Documented patterns for incorporating Devin into the SDLC: DevOps / CI loops, deployment workflows, release automation.

name: devin.product.deployment-capabilities
observations: Deployment capabilities: Devin's capacity to drive deploy/release automation — typically through SCM integrations + CI integration.

name: devin.product.essential-instructing
observations: Instructing Devin Effectively: Essential-guideline doc on prompt-engineering for Devin sessions. Companion to the good-vs-bad-instructions and when-to-use-Devin docs.

name: devin.product.good-vs-bad-instructions
observations: Good vs Bad Instructions: Essential-guideline doc contrasting effective vs ineffective task framing.

name: devin.product.when-to-use-devin
observations: When to Use Devin: Essential-guideline doc on selecting tasks suited to agent execution. Covers task scoping, complexity calibration.

name: devin.product.deepwiki-feature
observations: DeepWiki (Devin-generated repo docs): AI-generated documentation surface for any repo. Open-source at https://github.com/CognitionAI/deepwiki. Depends on repository indexing. DeepWiki MCP server (mcp.deepwiki.com) provides public-repo programmatic access.

name: devin.product.swebench-results
observations: SWE-bench results / harness: Cognition's published benchmark results on SWE-bench. Repository at github.com/CognitionAI/devin-swebench-results includes per-eval JSON results + harness. Used as a public benchmark reference for Devin's capability progression.

name: devin.product.agent-trace-spec
observations: Agent Trace (open spec): Cognition-published open specification for the context graph of code that an agent traces during a session. Open vendor-neutral spec.

name: devin.product.devin-2
observations: Devin 2.0 (April 2025): Major Devin release (April 3, 2025). Introduced product-level upgrades documented in the Devin 2 blog post.

name: devin.product.devin-2-2
observations: Devin 2.2 (Feb 24, 2026): Latest major Devin release. Feature deltas captured in the 2026 release notes.

name: devin.product.devin-agent-preview-sonnet-4-5
observations: Devin Agent Preview (Sonnet 4.5): September 29, 2025 release. Devin's agent preview running on Anthropic Sonnet 4.5.

name: devin.product.devin-2-1
observations: Devin 2.1 (May 15, 2025): May 15, 2025 release. Documented in the 2025 release notes.

name: devin.product.devin-can-schedule-devins
observations: Devin can now Schedule Devins (March 20, 2026): March 20, 2026 release. Adds cron-driven session scheduling.

name: devin.product.devin-can-manage-devins
observations: Devin can now Manage Devins (March 19, 2026): March 19, 2026 release. Coordinator pattern: a parent Devin spawns and manages subordinate Devin sessions.

name: devin.product.devin-in-windsurf
observations: Devin in Windsurf (April 15, 2026): April 15, 2026 release. Devin agent capabilities surfaced inside the Windsurf IDE.

name: devin.product.codemaps
observations: Windsurf Codemaps (Nov 4, 2025): Cognition feature surfaced via Windsurf for understanding code before edit. November 4, 2025 release.

name: devin.product.ai-data-analyst
observations: AI Data Analyst (Aug 2025): August 28, 2025 release. Devin used as a data-analyst — typically connected to database MCPs for ad-hoc analytics.

name: devin.product.deepwiki-launch
observations: DeepWiki: AI docs for any repo (May 5, 2025): May 5, 2025 release of DeepWiki — AI-generated documentation tooling.

name: devin.product.deepwiki-mcp-launch
observations: DeepWiki MCP Server (May 22, 2025): May 22, 2025. Launched the no-auth public-repo MCP server at mcp.deepwiki.com.

name: devin.product.audio-messages-slack
observations: Audio messages in Slack (Jan 2025): January 2025 product update. Devin can respond to audio messages sent via Slack — triggers session via voice clip.

name: devin.product.usage-based-billing-launch
observations: Usage-based billing (January 9, 2025): January 9, 2025. Launched pay-as-you-go billing with Additional Usage Budget cap. Bills at end of cycle OR when usage exceeds $2,000 (whichever comes first).

name: devin.product.enterprise-accounts-launch
observations: Enterprise Accounts (Jan 2025): January 2025 release. Enterprise accounts enable centralized management of multiple Devin organizations — admin, billing, member access controls.

name: devin.product.cloud-agents-blog
observations: What We Learned Building Cloud Agents (blog): Cognition blog post covering DevBox isolation, hypervisor snapshotting, async-gap survival, and the orchestration/governance/integration triad. Foundational architecture overview.

name: devin.product.how-cognition-uses-devin
observations: How Cognition Uses Devin to Build Devin (blog): Cognition's own usage patterns + internal MCP integrations. Real-world fluency-building reference.

name: devin.product.itau-case-study
observations: Itaú case study (17K engineers, 11mo): Customer case study cited in the Cloud Agents blog. Itaú (largest private bank in Latin America), 11 months in with ~17,000 engineers: 5–6× faster migrations, 70% auto-remediation of static-analysis security vulnerabilities, 2× test-coverage increase.

name: devin.product.engineer-fluency
observations: Engineer fluency (operational concept): Skill engineers develop by managing concurrent agent sessions over months on real projects. Distinct from writing code. Measured fluency comes from delegating + reviewing at scale.

name: devin.product.review-volume-shift
observations: Review-volume shift (org-process implication): When agents do significant share of execution, code review volume increases dramatically. Review processes designed for human-authored code don't transfer cleanly. Teams must establish what rigorous review looks like at higher volume.

name: devin.product.session-acu-soft-cap
observations: 10-ACU per-session soft cap: Cognition's recommended per-session ACU ceiling. Performance noticeably degrades beyond ~10 ACU. Soft (product nudges, doesn't enforce).

name: devin.product.bug-catcher-confidence-levels
observations: Devin Review bug-catcher confidence levels: Devin Review bug-catcher labels detected bugs by confidence. 'Severe' bugs require immediate attention. Lower-confidence bugs surfaced as flags.

name: devin.product.smart-diff-organization
observations: Smart diff organization (Devin Review): Devin Review groups changes logically (related edits together) instead of alphabetical. Makes large PRs more navigable.

name: devin.product.copy-move-detection
observations: Copy/move detection (Devin Review): Devin Review detects when code has been copied or moved and displays as a copy/move instead of full delete + insert. Reduces noise in refactor PRs.

name: devin.product.codebase-aware-chat
observations: Codebase-aware chat (Devin Review): PR-level chat that pulls in context from the rest of the codebase. Can ask Devin from any comment, bug, or flag in the diff view.

name: devin.product.code-changes-from-chat
observations: Code changes from chat (Devin Review): Ask Devin Review's chat to make code edits; review the suggested changes; apply as a commit to the PR branch without leaving the surface.

name: devin.product.pr-workflow-actions
observations: PR workflow actions (Devin Review): Merge / close / convert-to-draft / mark-ready-for-review / toggle-auto-merge directly from Devin Review. No need to switch to GitHub.

name: devin.product.review-github-compat
observations: GitHub compatibility (Devin Review): Devin Review's comments / approvals / change-requests sync back to GitHub bidirectionally. Supports GitHub Cloud + GitHub Enterprise Server.

name: devin.product.docs-sitemap
observations: docs.devin.ai sitemap.xml: Master URL inventory at https://docs.devin.ai/sitemap.xml. ~264 KB at fetch time. Used by Phase 1 ingest to enumerate Mintlify pages.

name: devin.product.docs-llms-txt
observations: docs.devin.ai llms.txt: AI-friendly index at https://docs.devin.ai/llms.txt. ~52 KB. Lists all available pages — used by AI agents to discover the documentation structure.

name: devin.product.release-notes-2024
observations: Release notes — 2024: 2024 release notes covering June 2024, September 2024, December 2024 (parts 1 + 2) updates. ~24 KB.

name: devin.product.release-notes-2025
observations: Release notes — 2025: 2025 release notes — biggest year for new features (DeepWiki, Devin 2.0/2.1, Sonnet 4.5 preview, audio in Slack, enterprise accounts, AI Data Analyst, Codemaps, Devin Review, multi-agent updates). ~47 KB.

name: devin.product.release-notes-2026
observations: Release notes — 2026: 2026 release notes — Devin can Manage Devins, Devin can Schedule Devins, Devin in Windsurf, Devin 2.2, Devin for Terminal. ~40 KB.

name: devin.product.deepwiki-readme
observations: CognitionAI/deepwiki repo: Open-source companion to DeepWiki (license unverified at fetch time; treated as private-corpus-only ingest). Supplements docs with implementation detail.

name: devin.product.user-best-practices
observations: User best practices (limitations, hallucinations, branch protection): Documented user-side guardrails. Devin may hallucinate, introduce bugs, or suggest insecure code. Recommended: code reviews, branch protections, standard org review processes.

name: devin.product.session-keyword-cheatsheet
observations: Session inline-keyword cheatsheet: Session-control keywords usable in Slack/Teams: !ask, !deep, mute, unmute, sleep, archive, EXIT, (aside), help; plus Slack-specific !dana, !fast, ![macro_name].

name: devin.knowledge-playbooks.knowledge-source
observations: Knowledge source (org/enterprise): Persistent context blob Devin uses across sessions. Fields: name, trigger, body. Three tiers: org, enterprise, repo. Per-repo: Devin only sees knowledge entries for the repo it's working on.

name: devin.knowledge-playbooks.knowledge-onboarding
observations: Knowledge onboarding (uploading knowledge to Devin): Initial process to populate Devin's knowledge base for a repo or org. Documented at /onboard-devin/knowledge-onboarding.

name: devin.knowledge-playbooks.playbook-creating
observations: Playbook (creating): Reusable instruction set encoded once and triggered by name/macro across surfaces (Slack/Teams/Jira/Linear). Fields: name, instructions, optional macro (e.g., `!plan`).

name: devin.knowledge-playbooks.playbook-using
observations: Playbook (using): Trigger paths: assign ticket to Devin (default playbook), label macro (`!plan`/`!implement`/`!triage`/`!review`), Slack/Teams keyword `![macro]`, or `assign + comment` flows.

name: devin.knowledge-playbooks.playbook-macro
observations: Playbook macro identifier: Optional `!`-prefixed identifier on a playbook. Required for label-based triggers in Jira/Linear and Slack-keyword triggers like `![ship-it]`.

name: devin.knowledge-playbooks.default-playbook
observations: Default playbook (per integration): Per-integration setting for which playbook fires when triggered without a specific macro. Linear default for new connections: `!plan`. Configurable in Jira/Linear settings.

name: devin.knowledge-playbooks.knowledge-trigger-field
observations: Knowledge `trigger` field: Knowledge note field describing WHEN the knowledge applies. Devin surfaces matching knowledge into context based on trigger relevance.

name: devin.knowledge-playbooks.knowledge-folder
observations: Knowledge folder (structure): Hierarchical folder structure for knowledge notes. Both org and enterprise scope. Folder structure with note counts retrievable via API.

name: devin.knowledge-playbooks.knowledge-suggestion
observations: Knowledge suggestion (pending): AI-generated suggestion for new knowledge entries based on observed session patterns. List/view/dismiss via the devin_knowledge_manage MCP tool.

name: devin.knowledge-playbooks.secret-resource
observations: Secret: Stored credential referenced as $VARIABLE_NAME from blueprints, sessions, and playbooks. Three tiers (enterprise, org, repo) with cascading precedence (more specific wins on name collision).

name: devin.knowledge-playbooks.secret-rotation
observations: Secret rotation: Rotate by deleting old + creating new (or by upserting in UI). New value takes effect on the next build for blueprint-referenced secrets. Recommended best practice: regular rotation cadence.

name: devin.knowledge-playbooks.secret-cascade-precedence
observations: Secret cascade precedence: Secrets cascade enterprise → org → repo with more specific tiers winning on name collision. Use intentionally to override enterprise defaults at the team level.

name: devin.knowledge-playbooks.secret-naming
observations: Secret naming convention: Best-practice: use descriptive names like `INTERNAL_NPM_TOKEN`, not `TOKEN_1`. Avoids confusion across multiple admins and over time.

name: devin.knowledge-playbooks.secret-no-yaml-rule
observations: Never put secrets in YAML rule: Strong best-practice: NEVER put secrets directly in blueprint YAML. Secrets in YAML end up in logs, build artifacts, and audit trails. Use the secrets management UI instead.

name: devin.knowledge-playbooks.secret-audit
observations: Secret audit (periodic review): Best-practice: periodically review which secrets exist and whether they're still needed. Remove unused secrets to reduce attack surface.

name: devin.knowledge-playbooks.knowledge-additive-across-tiers
observations: Knowledge additivity across blueprint tiers: Knowledge items are additive across enterprise/org/repo tiers. Devin sees all of them. Multiple tiers can define same-named knowledge items without overwriting.

name: devin.knowledge-playbooks.playbook-instructions
observations: Playbook `instructions` field: Body of a playbook. Free-form text describing what Devin should do when the playbook fires.

name: devin.knowledge-playbooks.playbook-mcp-management
observations: Programmatic playbook management (devin_playbook_manage): MCP tool exposed by Devin MCP for full CRUD on playbooks (list/get/create/update/delete) including macro support. Org-level + enterprise-level.

name: devin.knowledge-playbooks.knowledge-mcp-management
observations: Programmatic knowledge management (devin_knowledge_manage): MCP tool exposed by Devin MCP for full CRUD on knowledge notes + suggestions (list/get/create/update/delete; browse folder structure; manage suggestions). Filterable by repo/folder/search.

name: devin.product.devin-review
observations: Devin Review (code review platform): Full-service code review surface inside the Devin webapp. Smart diff organization, copy/move detection, bug catcher (with confidence levels), GitHub-compatible comment/approve/request-changes, codebase-aware chat, PR workflow actions (merge/close/draft/auto-merge), code-changes-from-chat. Supports GitHub Cloud + GitHub Enterprise Server. Surface URL: app.devin.ai/review.

name: methodology.ad-hoc-checklist-method
observations: Ad Hoc Checklist Method: Run-A-If-B-Do-C style checklist: site- or service-specific lists of known signals to inspect. Complementary to the USE Method's per-resource checklist.

name: methodology.intel-top-down
observations: Intel Hierarchical Top-Down Performance Characterization: CPU-pipeline-aware methodology: are UOPs issued? if yes, are they retired (good) or bad-speculation? if not, allocation stall → back-end vs front-end stalls. From Ahmad Yasin (Intel), in the IA-32 Optimization Reference Manual B.3.2.

name: methodology.tools-method
observations: Tools Method: List available performance tools, list the useful metrics each provides, list possible interpretations of each metric, then run selected tools and interpret. Tool-centric counterpart to the USE Method's resource-centric approach.

name: methodology.performance-evaluation-steps
observations: Performance Evaluation Steps: Ten-step performance-study procedure: state goals + system boundaries; list services + outcomes; select metrics; list parameters; select factors + values; select workload; design experiments; analyze data; present results; iterate. From Jain 1991.

name: methodology.tsa-method
observations: TSA Method: Thread State Analysis. For each thread of interest, measure time spent in each operating system thread state (Executing, Runnable, Swapping, Sleeping, Lock, Idle), then investigate states from most to least frequent using appropriate tools.

name: methodology.utilization
observations: Utilization: Fraction of time a resource was busy servicing work, or for storage resources the fraction of capacity used. The first of the three USE-Method questions for every resource.

name: methodology.rtfm-method
observations: RTFM Method: Read The Fine Manual: when researching performance tools and metrics, consult man pages, books, web search, co-workers, prior talk slides/video, support services, source code, experimentation, and social media — in roughly that order.

name: methodology.time-division-method
observations: Time Division Method: Measure operation time (or latency), divide it into logical synchronous components, continue dividing until the latency origin is identified, then quantify the speedup if it's fixed. Formerly called the Latency Analysis Method.

name: methodology.performance-mantras
observations: Performance Mantras: Don't do it. Do it, but don't do it again. Do it less. Do it later. Do it when they're not looking. Do it concurrently. Do it cheaper. Hierarchy of optimization preferences from Craig Hanson and Pat Crain.

name: methodology.request-rate
observations: Request Rate: Number of requests per second handled by a service. The 'R' in RED. Pairs with errors and duration to characterize service health.

name: methodology.problem-statement-method
observations: Problem Statement Method: Establish a clear problem statement before diving into analysis: What makes you think there's a performance problem? Has this system ever performed well? What changed recently? Can the degradation be expressed as latency or run time? Does it affect others? What is the environment? Sun Microsystems origin.

name: methodology.method-r
observations: Method R: Select user actions that matter for the business workload, measure causes of response time for those actions, calculate the best net-payoff optimization, and tune if the gain is sufficient. From Millsap & Holt's Optimizing Oracle Performance (2003).

name: methodology.cpu-flame-graph
observations: CPU Flame Graph: Flame graph variant generated from CPU stack profile data (typical: perf record + flamegraph.pl). The original variant — debugging on-CPU code paths.

name: methodology.by-layer-method
observations: By-Layer Method: Measure latency at each layer of the stack — dynamic languages, executable, libraries, syscalls, kernel (FS, network), device drivers — and investigate the lowest layer that introduces latency. Latency-tracing companion to USE.

name: methodology.capacity-planning-process
observations: Capacity Planning Process: Instrument the system, monitor system usage, characterize workload, predict performance under different alternatives, and select the lowest-cost / highest-performance alternative. From Jain 1991.

name: methodology.streetlight-anti-method
observations: Streetlight Anti-Method: Picking observability tools because they're familiar, found on the Internet, or found at random — then running them and looking for obvious issues. Named after the streetlight effect; documented as a bug, not a feature.

name: methodology.drunk-man-anti-method
observations: Drunk Man Anti-Method: Change things at random until the problem goes away. Plays well with confirmation bias and rarely identifies root cause.

name: methodology.random-change-anti-method
observations: Random Change Anti-Method: Measure baseline, change a random tunable in one direction, measure; change in the other direction, measure; keep whichever was better. Methodical version of the Drunk Man — still anti, because it doesn't ask why.

name: methodology.5-whys
observations: 5 Whys Performance Method: Given delivered performance, ask 'why?' and answer; given the previous answer, ask 'why?' again; repeat up to five times. Drives root-cause discovery beyond surface symptoms.

name: methodology.ooda-loop
observations: OODA Loop: Observe, Orient, Decide, Act. Decision-cycle methodology from John Boyd (US Air Force), popularized in technology by Roy Rapoport at Netflix. Useful for incident response cadence.

name: methodology.error-rate
observations: Error Rate: Count or rate of error events for a resource (USE) or service (RED). Errors are often present even when utilization and latency are healthy and represent the cleanest signal of a real problem.

name: methodology.off-cpu-analysis
observations: Off-CPU Analysis: Methodology for analyzing thread-wait latency: profile per-thread off-CPU time with stack traces, coalesce times with like stacks, and study stacks from largest to shortest. Surfaces blocked-thread time that on-CPU profiling misses. Application stack traces don't change while off-CPU, so a single sample at the end of the off-CPU period captures the wait context.

name: methodology.drill-down-analysis
observations: Drill-Down Analysis Method: Start at the highest level, examine next-level details, pick the most interesting breakdown, and recurse until the problem is solved. The default top-down decomposition pattern for performance investigation.

name: methodology.passive-benchmarking-anti-method
observations: Passive Benchmarking Anti-Method: Pick a benchmark tool, run it with a variety of options, slide-deck the results, hand to management. The anti-pattern that Active Benchmarking corrects.

name: methodology.red-method
observations: RED Method: For every service or microservice, check Request rate, Errors, and Duration. Service-oriented counterpart to USE; introduced by Tom Wilkie at Weaveworks. Pairs with the Four Golden Signals from Google SRE.

name: methodology.scientific-method
observations: Scientific Method (Performance): Question, Hypothesis, Prediction, Test, Analysis. Apply the standard scientific cycle to performance investigation — formulate a falsifiable hypothesis before measuring.

name: methodology.saturation
observations: Saturation: Degree to which a resource has extra work it can't service — typically measured by queue length or wait time. The second of the three USE-Method questions; surfaces issues hidden by sub-100% utilization.

name: methodology.duration
observations: Duration: How long a request takes. The 'D' in RED. Distribution matters — track tail latency (p95, p99) not just mean.

name: methodology.active-benchmarking
observations: Active Benchmarking Method: Configure the benchmark to run for a long duration; while it runs, analyze performance using other tools to determine the limiting factor. Counterpart to the Passive Benchmarking Anti-Method.

name: methodology.traffic-light-anti-method
observations: Traffic Light Anti-Method: Open a dashboard; if all green, assume everything is good; if something is red, assume that's the problem. Discounts both green-but-broken and red-but-irrelevant signals.

name: methodology.use-method
observations: USE Method: For every resource, check Utilization, Saturation, and Errors. Brendan Gregg's checklist-driven methodology for finding resource bottlenecks: iterate the resource list, ask the three questions, follow the signal. First in print in Gregg 2013 (CACM).

name: methodology.blame-someone-else-anti-method
observations: Blame-Someone-Else Anti-Method: Find a system or environment component you are not responsible for; hypothesize that the issue is there; redirect to the responsible team; when proven wrong, repeat. The anti-pattern that motivates owning the investigation.

name: methodology.cpu-profile-method
observations: CPU Profile Method: Generate a CPU profile (ideally a CPU flame graph) and understand all software in the profile that occupies more than ~1% of samples. Counterpart to off-CPU analysis for on-CPU work.

name: methodology.stack-profile-method
observations: Stack Profile Method: Profile thread stack traces both on- and off-CPU, coalesce, then study stacks bottom-up. A unified extension of CPU + off-CPU profiling.

name: methodology.workload-characterization
observations: Workload Characterization Method: Answer four questions: Who is causing the load? Why is the load called? What is the load? How is the load changing over time? Apply before tuning to ensure you're optimizing the right thing.

name: methodology.process-of-elimination
observations: Process of Elimination: Divide the target into components, choose a test that exonerates many untested components quickly, perform the test, recurse on remaining unknowns. Binary-search-style narrowing.

name: methodology.benchmarking-checklist
observations: Benchmarking Checklist: Six-question sanity check before trusting a benchmark: Why not double? Did it break limits? Did it error? Does it reproduce? Does it matter? Did it even happen? From Brendan Gregg.

name: methodology.flamescope
observations: FlameScope: Performance analysis tool by Brendan Gregg + Martin Spier (Netflix) that visualizes profiles as subsecond-offset heat maps and lets the user select time ranges to render as flame graphs. Reveals variation, perturbations, and periodic activity that aggregate flame graphs hide.

name: methodology.off-cpu-time
observations: Off-CPU Time: Time a thread spent waiting off-CPU (blocked on I/O, locks, timers, scheduler queues, paging) rather than running. Measurable as totals via /proc statistics or per-event via tracers like the bcc cpudist tool (-O mode).

name: methodology.bpftrace
observations: bpftrace: High-level tracing language and frontend for eBPF, modeled on AWK/DTrace. Recommended for one-liners and short scripts. github.com/iovisor/bpftrace.

name: methodology.icicle-chart
observations: Icicle Chart: Flame graph upside-down: y-axis grows downward from the root frame at the top. Useful when stacks are very deep — the initial view shows the bulk of the profile without scrolling. Generated via flamegraph.pl --inverted.

name: methodology.kprobe
observations: Kprobe: Linux kernel dynamic-tracing primitive: instrument any kernel function entry (kprobe) or return (kretprobe) at runtime by overwriting the first instruction with a breakpoint trap. Used by eBPF, ftrace, perf, SystemTap. Brittle across kernel versions because function names change.

name: methodology.bpf-verifier
observations: BPF Verifier: Kernel component that statically validates BPF bytecode before allowing it to run: rejects programs with loops, backwards branches, unbounded execution, or unsafe memory access. The reason BPF is safe to load from user-space.

name: methodology.cachestat
observations: cachestat: Linux page cache hit/miss/dirty statistics, summarized per second. Surfaces page-cache effectiveness — a low hit rate can mean working-set > RAM or anti-pattern access. Available in both bcc and perf-tools flavors.

name: methodology.flame-graph
observations: Flame Graph: Visualization of stack-trace-sampled profile data: x-axis is alphabetically-sorted sample population (NOT time), y-axis is stack depth from bottom. Wider rectangles = more frequent stacks. Top edge = on-CPU; below = ancestry. Created by Brendan Gregg in 2011 to debug a MySQL CPU issue. Implemented by flamegraph.pl and 100+ other tools.

name: methodology.off-cpu-tracing
observations: Off-CPU Tracing: Off-CPU analysis approach that traces every kernel context switch (e.g., finish_task_switch on Linux) with stack traces and timestamps, then aggregates by stack to compute per-stack off-CPU time. Captures all wait events for any application without per-app instrumentation.

name: methodology.uprobe
observations: Uprobe: User-level dynamic tracing primitive: attach to any user function entry/return at runtime. Has higher overhead than kprobes (~10x) since context switches across the user/kernel boundary on every event.

name: methodology.execsnoop
observations: execsnoop: Trace new processes via the exec() syscall, printing PID, parent PID, command, and arguments live as they run. Available in both bcc/eBPF and perf-tools/ftrace flavors. Essential for catching short-lived processes invisible to top/ps.

name: methodology.funccount
observations: funccount: Count kernel (or user) function calls matched by a wildcard pattern. Discovery tool: which TCP send paths fired? which VFS calls happened? -p filters by PID. bcc and perf-tools flavors.

name: methodology.off-cpu-flame-graph
observations: Off-CPU Flame Graph: Flame graph variant rendering off-CPU time (where threads were blocked) sampled with stack traces. Identifies blocking code paths. Yichun Zhang (2013) introduced the concept.

name: methodology.ftrace
observations: ftrace: Linux's built-in static + dynamic tracing framework, exposed via /sys/kernel/debug/tracing. Predates eBPF; the perf-tools wrapper scripts use it. Underrated — many capabilities aren't exposed via perf_events but are reachable through ftrace directly.

name: methodology.biolatency
observations: biolatency: Block I/O latency as a power-of-2 histogram (bcc/eBPF). Reveals bimodal distributions and tail latency that mean-latency metrics hide. -D mode breaks down by disk; -m for milliseconds. Fundamental disk-investigation tool.

name: methodology.tcpconnect
observations: tcpconnect: bcc/eBPF tool tracing TCP active connections (connect() syscall) with PID, IP, port. Pairs with tcpaccept (passive connections) and tcplife (per-connection lifetime).

name: methodology.memory-leak-flame-graph
observations: Memory Leak Flame Graph: Flame graph variant where stacks are sampled at byte-allocation events instead of CPU samples; width = bytes allocated. Identifies code paths responsible for memory growth or leaks. Colored green by convention to distinguish from CPU flame graphs.

name: methodology.off-cpu-sampling
observations: Off-CPU Sampling: Off-CPU analysis approach that samples blocked-thread stacks at a timer interval (or via a wall-time profiler that filters to off-CPU stacks). Lower fidelity than tracing but bounded overhead; rarely used by system profilers because of per-thread sampling cost.

name: methodology.usdt
observations: USDT: User Statically Defined Tracing — application-embedded probe points that user-space tracers can attach to. Like tracepoints but for user-space apps. Compiled in via DTrace-style probe macros; visible to BCC, bpftrace, SystemTap.

name: methodology.cpu-utilization-misleading
observations: CPU Utilization is Misleading: %CPU as reported by top(1) and most monitoring tools is really 'non-idle time' — it includes cycles stalled on memory I/O, which now dominate modern workloads. High %CPU often means the memory subsystem is the bottleneck, not the CPU package. Pair %CPU with IPC (or PMC stalled-cycles metrics) before tuning.

name: methodology.flame-chart
observations: Flame Chart: Time-on-x-axis variant of flame graphs, first added by Google Chrome's WebKit Web Inspector. Studies time-based patterns rather than aggregate hot paths. Distinct from flame graphs (which sort x by alphabet to maximize frame merging) — both are useful.

name: methodology.context-switch
observations: Context Switch: Kernel-scheduler event that swaps the running thread on a CPU. Off-CPU tracing instruments the function that finishes a context switch (Linux: finish_task_switch). Voluntary switches happen on blocking calls; involuntary ones happen under CPU pressure or interrupts.

name: methodology.ebpf
observations: Extended BPF: Linux 4.x extension of classic BPF: lets the in-kernel BPF VM run on events other than packets and do actions other than filtering. Programs are written in C, compiled to BPF bytecode, verified by the kernel verifier (no loops or backwards branches), then attached to event sources (kprobes, uprobes, tracepoints, perf_events). Used for tracing, security, software-defined networks, XDP.

name: methodology.ipc
observations: Instructions Per Cycle: Number of CPU instructions retired per clock cycle, averaged over a window. Brendan Gregg's rule of thumb: IPC < 1.0 → likely memory-stalled (tune memory I/O, caching, NUMA locality); IPC > 1.0 → instruction-bound (reduce code execution, look at CPU flame graphs). Modern Intel CPUs can retire 4 instructions per cycle ('4-wide').

name: methodology.profile
observations: profile: bcc/eBPF tool for timed CPU stack-trace sampling. -F sets frequency (typical: 49 Hz to dodge timer alignment); -d emits delimited frames; folded output goes straight to flamegraph.pl. Replaces perf record + perf script for most flame-graph workflows on Linux 4.9+.

name: methodology.pmc
observations: Performance Monitoring Counters: Hardware counters in modern CPUs that tally microarchitectural events: cycles, instructions, cache misses, branch mispredicts, stalled cycles, etc. Read via perf stat. The only honest way to know whether a CPU is instruction-bound vs memory-stalled.

name: methodology.biosnoop
observations: biosnoop: Per-event block I/O tracer (bcc/eBPF) showing time, comm, PID, disk, R/W, sector, bytes, and latency for every I/O. Use when biolatency's histogram identifies outliers and you need to attribute them to a specific process.

name: methodology.tcpretrans
observations: tcpretrans: Trace TCP retransmits with addresses, ports, and TCP state. Surfaces network reliability issues without the overhead of tracing every send/receive (since retransmits are typically <<1% of traffic). Both bcc and perf-tools flavors.

name: methodology.bpf
observations: Berkeley Packet Filter: In-kernel sandboxed virtual machine originally designed for tcpdump-style packet filtering. tcpdump expressions compile to BPF bytecode that the VM executes. Predecessor of eBPF.

name: methodology.tracepoint
observations: Tracepoint: Static kernel tracing instrumentation point — placed by kernel developers and exposed under /sys/kernel/debug/tracing/events. Stable interface across kernel versions, unlike kprobes. Examples: block:block_rq_insert, sched:sched_switch, syscalls:sys_enter_*.

name: methodology.libbpf
observations: libbpf: Modern C library for loading BPF programs into the kernel — pairs with BTF (BPF Type Format) and CO-RE (Compile Once, Run Everywhere) for portable programs. Replaces the BCC Python toolchain for production-grade tools (per Brendan Gregg's 2020 update).

name: methodology.bcc
observations: BPF Compiler Collection: Collection of eBPF tracing tools and a C/Python/Lua frontend for writing more (github.com/iovisor/bcc). Recommended for complex tools and daemons. Provides 100+ ready-to-run tools (execsnoop, opensnoop, biolatency, etc.). The Python interface is now considered deprecated in favor of libbpf+CO-RE.

name: methodology.bpf-map
observations: BPF Map: In-kernel data structure (array, hash, histogram, stack-trace, etc.) used by eBPF programs to store state and pass data to user-space. Doing in-kernel summarization via maps is what makes eBPF tracing efficient — much lower overhead than dumping every event.

name: methodology.iosnoop
observations: iosnoop: perf-tools/ftrace counterpart to biosnoop: trace disk I/O events with latency. Older Linux kernels (3.2+) where eBPF isn't available. The biosnoop bcc tool supersedes it on modern kernels.

name: methodology.differential-flame-graph
observations: Differential Flame Graph: Flame graph variant for comparing two profiles (e.g., regression testing) by coloring frames red/blue based on which profile contributed more samples. Surfaces what changed between two states.

name: methodology.frame-pointer
observations: Frame Pointer: Register (e.g., RBP on x86_64) holding the previous stack frame's base address. Required by frame-pointer-based stack walkers (perf, eBPF). The -fomit-frame-pointer compiler flag breaks this; Java needs -XX:+PreserveFramePointer (added in JDK 8u60 + JDK 9) to preserve it.

name: methodology.opensnoop
observations: opensnoop: Trace open() syscalls printing process name and full path. Identifies which processes are reading which files (useful for config-file discovery, missing-file diagnosis, and attribution). Both bcc and perf-tools versions.

name: methodology.runqlat
observations: runqlat: Run-queue latency histogram (bcc/eBPF): time threads spent waiting on the CPU run queue before being scheduled. High runqlat = CPU saturation in USE-method terms. Direct measurement of what 'CPU is busy' should mean.

name: methodology.stackcount
observations: stackcount: Count stack traces leading to a given function or tracepoint (bcc/eBPF). Answers 'who calls X?' across the kernel — useful for understanding which code paths trigger an event of interest.

name: methodology.perf-events
observations: perf_events: Linux's standard performance counter and tracing subsystem (also called 'perf'). Provides timed sampling, PMC reads, and tracepoint instrumentation. Frontend: the perf(1) command. Used as one of eBPF's event sources.

name: methodology.black-box-monitoring
observations: Black-Box Monitoring: Testing externally visible behavior as a user would see it. Symptom-oriented and active — 'the system isn't working correctly, right now'. Useless for not-yet-occurring imminent problems but ideal for paging discipline (only alert on real, ongoing user impact).

name: methodology.tail-latency
observations: Tail Latency: Latency of the slowest fraction of requests (e.g., p99, p99.9). Often dominates user experience because users hit several backends per page render — a 99th-percentile of one backend becomes the median for the frontend. Mean latency hides tail behavior; always track distributions.

name: methodology.yield
observations: Yield: Fraction of well-formed requests that succeed — synonym for availability when applied at request level. Per the SRE book's SLO chapter terminology.

name: methodology.action-item
observations: Action Item: Specific follow-up task from a postmortem with owner, priority, type (mitigate / prevent / process / other), and due date. Bug-fix-priority is review criterion. Action items are how postmortem learning translates to actual change.

name: methodology.monitoring
observations: Monitoring: Collecting, processing, aggregating, and displaying real-time quantitative data about a system: query counts, error counts, processing times, server lifetimes. Foundation for alerting, dashboards, debugging, and capacity planning.

name: methodology.sla
observations: Service Level Agreement: Explicit or implicit contract with users including consequences (financial or other) of meeting/missing SLOs. Distinguished from SLO: an SLO is a target; an SLA is what happens when the target is missed. A real 'SLA violation' would trigger breach-of-contract; most casual 'SLA violation' talk actually means missed SLO.

name: methodology.contributing-cause
observations: Contributing Cause: Factor that contributed to an incident. Plural by design — most incidents have multiple contributing causes (insufficient automation, software that crashed on bogus input, insufficient testing of the fix). Replaces the singular 'root cause' framing for systemic understanding.

name: methodology.durability
observations: Durability: Likelihood data will be retained over a long period — the storage-system counterpart to availability. Critical for storage SLIs alongside availability + latency.

name: methodology.postmortem-review
observations: Postmortem Review: Formal senior-engineer review of postmortem drafts: is incident data complete? are impact assessments thorough? was the root cause sufficiently deep? is the action plan appropriate? are bug-fix priorities right? was outcome shared with stakeholders? 'No postmortem left unreviewed.'

name: methodology.four-golden-signals
observations: Four Golden Signals: Latency, Traffic, Errors, Saturation. From Google SRE Book Ch. 6: 'If you can only measure four metrics of your user-facing system, focus on these four.' The canonical user-facing-service monitoring framework. Pairs with the USE Method (resources) and RED Method (service requests).

name: methodology.symptoms-vs-causes
observations: Symptoms vs Causes: A monitoring system should answer two distinct questions: what's broken (symptom) and why (cause). Pages should fire on symptoms (real user-visible impact); cause-oriented heuristics aid debugging but should not page. In multi-layered systems, one person's symptom is another person's cause.

name: methodology.percentile-latency
observations: Percentile Latency: Latency expressed as a percentile of the request distribution (median = p50; p90, p99, p99.9 increasingly stress the tail). User studies show people prefer slightly slower with low variance over fast-with-high-variance, so SLOs commonly target p99 or p99.9.

name: methodology.command-post
observations: Command Post: Recognized location where stakeholders can find the Incident Commander. Often a 'War Room' (physical or virtual). Google uses IRC + bots that log incident traffic and alerts to the channel — invaluable for postmortem reconstruction.

name: methodology.incident-state-document
observations: Live Incident State Document: Living document the IC maintains during an incident, editable by multiple people concurrently (Google Docs / wiki). Most-important info at the top. Retained for postmortem analysis. Should NOT depend on the software you're trying to fix.

name: methodology.page
observations: Page: A pager-routed alert demanding immediate human action. The most expensive class of alert because it interrupts on-call sleep/personal time. Per the SRE book: every page should be actionable, require intelligence, and represent a novel or unseen problem.

name: methodology.alert-fatigue
observations: Alert Fatigue: Pager fatigue / alert spam: when alerts fire too frequently, on-callers second-guess, skim, or ignore them — including real ones masked in the noise. Tracked via incidents-per-shift; mitigated by ruthlessly cutting low-signal alerts and tuning thresholds.

name: methodology.incident-command-system
observations: Incident Command System: Incident response framework derived from FEMA's National Incident Management System. Google's incident management is built on it. Scales smoothly via recursive separation of responsibilities — leaders can delegate by creating sub-incidents.

name: methodology.postmortem
observations: Postmortem: Written record of an incident, its impact, the actions taken to mitigate or resolve it, the root cause(s), and follow-up actions to prevent recurrence. Goals: ensure the incident is documented, all contributing causes are understood, effective preventive actions land. NOT punishment — a learning opportunity for the entire company.

name: methodology.error-budget
observations: Error Budget: Rate at which SLOs can be missed. 'An error budget is just an SLO for meeting other SLOs.' Used as input to release-cadence decisions: if budget remains, ship faster; if budget is exhausted, freeze and stabilize. Reframes reliability as a business resource, not an absolute.

name: methodology.qps
observations: Queries Per Second: Requests-per-second metric — typically determined by user demand, not chosen as an SLO. Pairs with latency: higher QPS often correlates with larger latency, with performance cliffs beyond a load threshold.

name: methodology.incident-declaration-criteria
observations: Incident Declaration Criteria: Per the SRE book, an event is an incident if any of: (1) you need a second team to fix it, (2) the outage is customer-visible, (3) it's unsolved after an hour of concentrated analysis. Better to declare early and close fast than spin up the framework hours into a problem.

name: methodology.sli
observations: Service Level Indicator: Carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of service level provided. Common SLIs: request latency, error rate, throughput, availability (well-formed requests that succeed), durability (likelihood of long-term retention). Aggregated over a measurement window into rate/average/percentile.

name: methodology.operations-lead
observations: Operations Lead: Works with the Incident Commander to apply operational tools to mitigate the incident. The Ops team is the only group authorized to modify the system during an incident — prevents the 'freelancing' anti-pattern.

name: methodology.dashboard
observations: Dashboard: Web-based summary view of a service's core metrics. Pre-built to surface the most important metrics; may include filters, ticket-queue length, on-call name, recent pushes. Per the SRE book, dashboards should answer basic service questions and normally include the Four Golden Signals.

name: methodology.incident-handoff
observations: Incident Handoff: Explicit transfer of Incident Commander role across time zones / shifts. Outgoing IC must verbally state 'You're now the incident commander, okay?' and not leave the call until firm acknowledgment. Communicated to all responders.

name: methodology.slo
observations: Service Level Objective: Target value or range for a service level measured by an SLI. Form: 'SLI ≤ target' or 'lower ≤ SLI ≤ upper'. Example: '99% of Get RPC calls will complete in less than 100 ms.' SLOs reflect what users care about; choosing them is product/business work, not pure engineering.

name: methodology.nines
observations: Nines: Shorthand notation for high-availability targets: '2 nines' = 99%, '3 nines' = 99.9%, '5 nines' = 99.999%. Each nine corresponds to ~10× less downtime: 5 nines ≈ 5 min/year, 4 nines ≈ 52 min/year, 3 nines ≈ 8.76 hr/year.

name: methodology.planning-lead
observations: Planning Lead: Supports Ops with longer-term issues during an incident: filing bugs, ordering dinner, arranging handoffs, tracking how the system has diverged from norm so it can be reverted on resolution.

name: methodology.recursive-separation-of-responsibilities
observations: Recursive Separation of Responsibilities: Incident response design pattern: every responder knows their role and doesn't stray onto someone else's. If a role's load is excessive, ask the planning lead for more staff or delegate to subordinates / sub-incidents. Counterintuitively, clear separation gives more autonomy than less — no second-guessing colleagues.

name: methodology.white-box-monitoring
observations: White-Box Monitoring: Monitoring based on metrics exposed by the internals of the system — logs, JVM Profiling Interface, HTTP /metrics endpoints. Allows detection of imminent problems and failures masked by retries. Sometimes symptom-oriented, sometimes cause-oriented depending on instrumentation depth.

name: methodology.alert
observations: Alert: A notification intended for a human, pushed to a system such as a bug/ticket queue, email alias, or pager. Classified by destination as tickets, email alerts, or pages.

name: methodology.wheel-of-misfortune
observations: Wheel of Misfortune: Disaster role-playing exercise: a previous postmortem is reenacted with engineers playing the roles. Original incident commander attends to make it realistic. Used to onboard new SREs and keep incident management skills sharp.

name: methodology.availability
observations: Availability: Fraction of time a service is usable, often defined as the fraction of well-formed requests that succeed. 100% is impossible, near-100% achievable; expressed as 'nines' (99% = 2 nines, 99.999% = 5 nines). Google Compute Engine target: 99.95% (three and a half nines).

name: methodology.postmortem-trigger
observations: Postmortem Trigger: Pre-defined criteria that mandate a postmortem. Common triggers: user-visible downtime above a threshold, data loss of any kind, on-call intervention (rollback, traffic rerouting), resolution time above threshold, monitoring failure (manual incident discovery). Define BEFORE incidents to avoid rationalization.

name: methodology.cascading-failure
observations: Cascading Failure: Failure that grows by overwhelming healthy components — typically when load spilled from a failed component overloads its neighbors, propagating. Classic origin pattern: lose 1 of 5 datacenters, the others can't handle 25% extra load and fall over in sequence. Mitigated by graceful degradation and load shedding.

name: methodology.incident-commander
observations: Incident Commander: Holds the high-level state about an incident; structures the response task force, assigns responsibilities, removes roadblocks for Ops. De facto holds all roles not delegated. The single accountable decision-maker during an incident.

name: methodology.communication-lead
observations: Communication Lead: Public face of the incident response task force. Issues periodic updates to the response team and stakeholders (typically email), keeps the incident document accurate and up to date. Removes communication burden from IC and Ops.

name: methodology.blameless-postmortem
observations: Blameless Postmortem: Postmortem that focuses on identifying systemic contributing causes without indicting individuals or teams. Originated in healthcare and avionics where mistakes can be fatal. Assumes everyone involved had good intentions and acted on the best info available — 'you can't fix people, you fix systems'. A cornerstone of SRE culture.

name: methodology.strace
observations: strace: Classic Linux user-space tool that traces syscalls made by a target process via the ptrace(2) interface. Very simple to use but has high overhead — every traced syscall causes two extra context switches. Per Julia Evans, often the favorite debugging tool despite the cost.

name: methodology.systemtap
observations: SystemTap: Pre-eBPF Linux tracing/scripting tool. Compiles a stap script into a kernel module loaded into the running kernel. Powerful and battle-tested but complex to set up; largely superseded by eBPF on modern kernels but still used on RHEL where stap has long-standing support.

name: methodology.dtrace
observations: DTrace: Sun/Solaris dynamic tracing system from 2003 — the conceptual ancestor of eBPF-based tracing. Uses static probe points (USDT-equivalent) and a custom scripting language (D). Available on illumos, FreeBSD, macOS; Linux port exists but is largely superseded by bpftrace + eBPF.

name: methodology.ltrace
observations: ltrace: Library-call tracer — traces calls into shared libraries (e.g., libc malloc, free, fopen) via ptrace. The library-level counterpart to strace's syscall view. Higher overhead than uprobes-based tools.

name: methodology.tracing-taxonomy
observations: Linux Tracing Taxonomy: Mental model from Julia Evans (with Brendan Gregg's framing) for Linux's tracing landscape: split into three layers — data sources (kprobes / uprobes / tracepoints / USDT), collection mechanisms (ftrace / perf_events / eBPF), and user frontends (perf, bcc, bpftrace, ftrace shell wrappers, LTTng, SystemTap). Most confusion in Linux tracing comes from conflating these layers.

name: methodology.lttng
observations: LTTng: Linux Trace Toolkit Next Generation — high-performance kernel + user-space tracing system from Polytechnique Montréal. Optimized for low overhead and large trace volumes. Includes lttng-ust for user-space tracepoints. Used heavily in academic + telecom contexts; less common in general SRE work.

name: firecracker.kvm.kvm-subsystem
observations: KVM (Kernel-based Virtual Machine): Linux kernel module exposing /dev/kvm; provides the hardware-virtualization primitives (VMX on Intel, SVM on AMD, EL2 on ARM) that Firecracker uses as its VMM substrate. Firecracker is a userspace VMM that talks to KVM via ioctls — KVM handles the heavy CPU/MMU virt; Firecracker handles devices, scheduling, and the API.

name: firecracker.kvm.system-fd
observations: KVM System fd: Handle obtained from open('/dev/kvm'). Used to issue system-level ioctls that affect the whole KVM subsystem (KVM_GET_API_VERSION, KVM_CHECK_EXTENSION, KVM_CREATE_VM, KVM_GET_VCPU_MMAP_SIZE, KVM_GET_MSR_INDEX_LIST). The first thing Firecracker opens at VMM init.

name: firecracker.kvm.vm-fd
observations: KVM VM fd: Handle returned by KVM_CREATE_VM on the system fd. Scopes ioctls to one virtual machine — memory layout, irqchip, MSI/IRQ routing, vCPU creation. VM ioctls must be issued from the same process (address space) that created the VM.

name: firecracker.kvm.vcpu-fd
observations: KVM vCPU fd: Handle returned by KVM_CREATE_VCPU on the VM fd. Scopes ioctls to a single virtual CPU — register state (regs/sregs/MSRs/CPUID/FPU/XSAVE), the KVM_RUN entry, LAPIC, MP state. vcpu ioctls should be issued from the thread that will run KVM_RUN; otherwise a thread-local cache may be flushed unnecessarily.

name: firecracker.kvm.device-fd
observations: KVM Device fd: Handle returned by KVM_CREATE_DEVICE. Scopes ioctls to in-kernel emulated devices (e.g. ARM GIC, PMU, vfio). Firecracker uses few in-kernel devices on x86 (most are VirtIO in userspace); on aarch64 the GIC is created via this path.

name: firecracker.kvm.kvm-run
observations: KVM_RUN main loop: The vCPU ioctl that enters the guest. Returns when the guest exits — to userspace via shared `kvm_run` mmap struct that carries the exit reason and any per-exit data (MMIO/PIO request, IRQ window, etc.). Firecracker runs one KVM_RUN main loop per vCPU thread; userspace handles the exit, resolves the I/O, and loops back into KVM_RUN.

name: firecracker.kvm.kvm-run-mmap
observations: kvm_run shared structure: Memory-mapped region (size obtained via KVM_GET_VCPU_MMAP_SIZE) shared between userspace and the kernel for one vCPU. Carries `exit_reason`, per-exit unions (mmio, io, internal, fail_entry, hyperv, system_event), and request flags. Userspace mmaps it once at vCPU init; the kernel writes to it on every KVM_RUN return.

name: firecracker.kvm.exit-mmio
observations: KVM_EXIT_MMIO: Guest accessed a memory range that wasn't backed by KVM_SET_USER_MEMORY_REGION. kvm_run.mmio carries phys_addr, len (1/2/4/8), data[8], is_write. Firecracker uses this to dispatch to its VirtIO device emulators (on aarch64 this is the primary device-MMIO transport; on x86 too for VirtIO-MMIO).

name: firecracker.kvm.exit-io
observations: KVM_EXIT_IO: Guest issued an I/O port instruction (in/out) on x86. kvm_run.io carries direction, size (1/2/4), port, count. Firecracker handles this for legacy serial (port 0x3f8), i8042 keyboard controller (0x60/0x64), and PIT/PIC ports — the minimal legacy device set.

name: firecracker.kvm.exit-shutdown
observations: KVM_EXIT_SHUTDOWN: Guest issued an architectural reset (triple-fault on x86, PSCI SYSTEM_OFF on ARM). Firecracker treats this as terminal — emits InstanceShutdown via state machine and tears down the microVM.
